en: *New Studies in the Names and Phrases of the Vinaya School*, Volume One (with Preface).
Within the *Vinaya*, the texts of the *Ekottarika-āgama* are fully enumerated, yet they do not comprehensively encompass all the various schools (*nikāya*).

Now, although one’s own school may extensively expound the numerical categories of the Dharma of the various vehicles, it nevertheless remains restricted to its own single lineage. This causes those among the late learners of our school to remain ignorant when it comes to [examining]...

I have examined [the texts] and found many omissions. During my leisure time from regular studies, I have freely engaged in discussion, synthesizing the phrases and passages from various sections and collecting the terminology of this single school.
I have compiled these into three fascicles to bequeath to beginners. Although I am unable to elucidate the great principles, I hope they may serve as a supplement to what has been forgotten.

Preface to the *Collection of Sentences and Phrases for New Students of the Vinaya School*, Volume One, compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaixian at the Fahuā Aranya on the day of the summer retreat at the beginning of the Shaoxing era.
The *Yilü Shichao* (Abridged Commentary on the Vinaya) follows the *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya); this Dharmaguptaka school belongs to the Mahāyāna.
The intent of the "One Person's Karmavācanā" (Ekapudgala-karmavācanā) is solely to rescue and deliver that single individual.
The *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* (Precept Text) of a single teacher is studied by all disciples together, blending like water and milk.
First, regarding the *Liyun* (Explanations of the Vinaya), it states that one should always maintain a single-minded focus on the thought of removing all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Second, the *Yinian jing* (Sutra on a Single Thought) states that when a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open.
Third, in the *Shishi chao* (Commentary on the Essentials of the Vinaya), beneath each individual matter, many points of established intent are set forth.
The One Vehicle Dharma Flower: throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle.
A single *tāla* tree is seven *ren* high.
A single lamp: for the sake of nursing the sick or rewarding labor, even down to lighting a single lamp.
One who skillfully understands the *Ekākṣara-nirvāṇa-sūtra* is called a Vinaya Master (*vinayadhara*).
The preface to the *Karmavācanā* points toward the ultimate goal to manifest the single principle.
Regarding "one son" and nirvana, one regards all sentient beings with the thought that they are identical to one's own only son.
The section on "Observance and Transgression" (*jìfàn zhīmén*) in the *Shūsō-ki* runs throughout the entire work.
Regarding the six ritual objects (*rokubutsu*), they are universally prescribed for use across all teachings;
thus, one should exchange them every ten days, mentally reciting the formula for purification (*setsujō*) and relinquishing the old to receive the new.
If the shadow passes even the length of a single hair [of a horse's tail], it is already considered "improper time" (*akāla*).
One *ren*—according to the *Xiaoya*: four chi is called one *ren*.
Regarding "one bowl": according to the *Jizhilun*, the food in one bowl causes a husband to break into a sweat.
Regarding the "Commentary on the Single Essence Precepts" (*Yiti jieshu*), it speaks of the "Single Essence of the Triple Gem.
As for the "Single Meaning," the *Vinaya* states that the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of this single meaning.
Regarding the "Single Eye," the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* (*Lunliao lun*) says that a person cherishes one eye with extreme gravity.
First, regarding the *Yeshiye shu* (Commentary on Karma): consciousness does not falsely perceive objects, but consists solely of a single consciousness.
Second, regarding the *Fang sengwang pian* (Chapter on the Monastic Net): one must be thorough in the establishment of laws for traveling and transforming others.
Third, regarding those who provide offerings: according to the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), there are sixty types of dhūta practices.
A *kṣaṇa* consists of twenty *nimeṣas*. One *fathom* (*xún*):
the *Xiǎoyǎ* states that twice a *zhèn* is called a *xún*.
One intercalary month: according to the *Jièshū*, this country uses a calendar that intercalates one month every three years.
In the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the section on the "One Article" mentions three coins each of gold and silver;
the "Once-returner" (*ekāgāmin*) asks me about the five hundred questions regarding non-extinction for half a month;
and in the *Shengdaojing* (Platform Sutra), it says that if one's mind lacks the Holy Dharma, one merely wastes a lifetime.
One *vitasti* is one foot for a human being, two feet for a Buddha.
One *karma-kṣetra* is that which projects one birth; many karmas can bring it to completion.
One *dhanus* is seven feet and two inches.
The *I-mon jissō* (One Article on the Reality of Affairs) clarifies that the fundamental reality of the Vinaya-piṭaka is as follows:
one *jin* (指) refers to a human finger, while one *sun* (寸) refers to two finger-widths of a Buddha.
"One disordering of the precept-commentary" means that the precepts and wholesome qualities have become confused into a single disorder.
A single section of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* is like a thick mat woven from many layers; when divided into its subsequent sections, it consists of five parts.
A single grain of the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is like a single grain of rice, which only after a hundred craftsmen’s labor can be fully formed.
A single reed: the *Platform Sūtra* spans the passes and rivers as if by a single reed.
One summer’s work: the *Commentary on the Precepts* and the recitation of the eighty sections of the Vinaya constitute the achievement of one summer.
A single verse: four lines constitute one verse.
One *krośa* according to the *Zabaozang jing* (Sūtra on the Treasury of Miscellaneous Jewels), five *li* according to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and two *li* according to one tradition;

one *sengtan* (monastic precinct) according to the *Sengtanjing* (Sūtra on Monastic Precincts), and six *wan* (ten thousand) years according to the *Sengjiejijing* (Sūtra on the Ordination of the Sangha).
To receive the precepts for a single lifetime is called "receiving them in vain," for it renders one's efforts futile and laborious for that entire life.
Regarding shaving, the *Vinaya* states that one should shave once every half-month; this is the constant rule.
One finger-snap (*acchaṭā*) consists of twenty eye-blinks (*nimeṣa*).
A single set of ceremonial robes; how could one set of the three robes suffice for both dusk and dawn?
One *li* consists of three hundred paces.
Regarding the "one rotation" mentioned in the *Jieshu*: within the womb, there is one rotation every seven days.
First, regarding the *Yujie shu* (Commentary on the Bathing Precepts): bathing once every half-month exceeds the limit of what is permitted by the rules.
Second, regarding the *Fojie shu* (Commentary on the Buddha’s Precepts): because there is only one Buddha in the world, this [rule] is eternally fixed.
Third, regarding the precept against false speech: it is said that many people are prone to violating this particular precept.
One *chi* according to the Tang regulations is one *cun* and two *fen*; in the Ji Zhou period, it was ten *cun*.

Regarding the "one cup," the *Hizhì jīng* (Scripture on Upholding the World) states that if one does not eliminate the inversion of self, one shall not be permitted to receive even a single cup of water.
Regarding the Vinaya commentaries of a single school, this particular school alone has not yet branched into sub-sects.
Within one lineage of Vinaya commentaries, there are two lineages—the Mahāsāṃghika and the Sthavira—and within these, two further lineages: the Kāśyapīya and the Dharmaguptaka.
Regarding the Vinaya commentaries of a single recitation, once false speech is uttered, it cannot be recovered even through a hundred attempts at repentance.
One jun is thirty jin. One yojana—
according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*— is eighty li for the superior grade, sixty li for the middle grade, and forty li for the inferior grade.
One step is six chi.
One cubit (hasta) is one chi eight cun, which is three chi six cun in Buddhist measurement.
One *paṭa* measures twenty-eight cubits.
Regarding the *Fenshi chao*: A single offense may still result in punishment, while multiple offenses necessarily require long kalpas [of retribution].
Regarding the *Yidu lun*: A single robe cannot ward off the cold, whereas the three robes can provide such protection.
Regarding the statement that "all those who have received the precepts" refers to those subject to the hundred obstacles who should not leave the household life:

the *Shenzhou Yitong Shichao* (The Comprehensive Record of the Unified Land of China) states that, concerning the reception [of precepts], one should recite the text from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü).
First, the dhūta practice of eating a single morsel of food does not yield benefit;
it is merely a violation of the transformative teachings (kaijō) that results in the retribution of a single karmic path.
First, the dhūta practice of eating only one meal a day.
1. A group of monks who keep cats and dogs as a collective practice is a group that lacks the precepts.
2. One *zhang* (in the *Zhilun*): the light of the Tathāgata’s body is one *zhang*.
3. One *xūyù* (in the *Sengqī*: twenty *luóyù*; in the *Abhidharmakośa*: thirty *lièbó*).
One *liang* consists of twenty-four *zhu*.
Regarding "one grain of wheat," the *Vinaya* states that a fingernail one grain long is a sign of breaking the precepts.
Regarding "one taste," the *Vinaya* states that when the waters of the ocean have all become salty, they constitute a single taste.
Regarding the simultaneous undertaking of many precepts, it is better to simultaneously undertake all the precepts than to simultaneously violate all of them.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one may keep the robes for a single night; according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this applies throughout the entire assembly, provided one faces the dawn.
In this single thread, the warp and woof of five parts are woven together; even a single strand passing through the center is uniformly cut and joined.
One portion is the Tathāgata’s ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft) within the Buddha-treasury, and one portion is offered to all the ordained disciples.
In the month of Kārttika there is clothing for one month, and in the five months of summer there is no clothing for one month.
According to one version of the *Benshō*, the "Manifestation of Worldly Practices" contains a hundred items, yet not a single one exists.
One *ki* consists of twelve years.
The *Yijia yeshu* (Outline of the One Family) is what the present-day Yijia school recites directly from the original text.
Regarding the initial reception of the precepts, it states that they differ from non-Buddhists in being received all at once (*yiwang dunsou*).
It further notes that for one kalpa, Devadatta fell into hell for drawing blood [from the Buddha], while for one kalpa, Jīvaka was born in heaven for drawing blood [from the Buddha].
The ascetic practice of eating in a single sitting and abstaining from light snacks;
it is easier to give up the position of a Wheel-Turning King in the future with a distracted mind than it is to refuse a single coin in the present.
Throughout one's entire life, the marks of renunciation are received, wherein non-action (avijñapti) is suspended and projected for the duration of that lifetime.
First, regarding the *Shou shi chao* (Notes on Receiving [the Precepts]): once one has received them, it is difficult and inappropriate to receive them again.

First, regarding the recitation of the reception: it requires a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for its acquisition, but only a single recitation is required for its relinquishment. Second, regarding the observance: there is the observance of restraint (*saṃvara*) and the observance of performance (*kriyā*).
Two are offenses of commission, one is an offense of omission, and two are offenses of action.
Two are not one; one is non-material, and one is non-mental.
Two are invitations to the Sangha as a whole, and one is an individual invitation.

The two commentaries are: first, the *Shiyao chao* (Essential Matters Commentary); second, the *Yi chao* (Meaning Commentary). The two sub-commentaries are: first, the *Jie shu* (Precepts Sub-commentary); second, the *Ye shu* (Karma Sub-commentary).
The two sections on robes are: first, robes prescribed by rule; second, robes permitted by concession.
The two truths: first, the ultimate truth; second, the conventional truth. The two vehicles:
first, the vehicle of the śrāvakas; second, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
The two practices: first, self-practice; second, collective practice.
There are two types of retribution: first, collective retribution; second, individual retribution. There are two kinds of teachers:
first, the preceptor (upādhyāya) who bestows virtue and precepts; second, the instructor (ācārya) upon whom one relies.
There are two aspects of being within the same boundary: first, residing in the same dwelling place; second, reciting the precepts together.
There are two types of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*): first, true purity; second, mutual purity.
There are two types of immediate succession (*anantara*): first, bodily immediacy; second, the immediacy of suffering.
Regarding the two types of precious precepts: first, the precept against hoarding precious things; second, the precept against trading precious things.
Regarding the two periods of instruction: first, the present life; second, the future life.
Regarding the two kinds of precepts: first, natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*); second, prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*).

Regarding the two meanings of committing a grave offense (which cannot be saved even by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas): first, the determination of the karma one has received; second, the determination of the karma one has performed.
There are two ways of relinquishing the precepts: first, by departing from the precept against sexual misconduct; second, by departing from the method of receiving the precepts.
Regarding the increase of the two types of wisdom: first, one who constantly observes the transgressions; second, one who is able to repent after having committed a transgression.
Two kinds of delusion (with two additions): first, not seeing one's transgressions; second, having committed a transgression and not confessing it.
Two kinds of nirvana: first, with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*); second, without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
The term *chao* (抄) has two meanings: first, the sense of "extracting" (採摘); second, the sense of "encompassing" (包攝).
The Buddha has two bodies (*pañcaśata-praśna*): first, the internal body; second, the Dharma-body.
Two dharmas can protect the world (*saṃyukta-āgama*): first, shame (*hrī*); second, dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
The Two Principles (*Zhouyi*): first, heaven; second, earth.
The Two Sequences: first, the general sequence; second, the specific sequence.
The Two Bonds (*Ratnakūṭa*): first, the bond of views; second, the bond of gain and honor.
The two types of frivolous speech are: first, frivolousness of body; second, frivolousness of speech.
The two kinds of obstacles are: first, the obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); second, the obstacle to life.
The two types of slander are: first, groundless slander; second, slander based on false grounds.
There are two types of death: first, the death of the fragmented [body];
second, the death of the transformative [body]. There are two kinds of dwellings: first, dwellings with an owner;
second, dwellings without an owner. There are two Vinaya traditions: first, the Sthavira school (within the cave); second, the Mahāsāṃghika school (outside the cave).
There are two types of schisms in the Saṃgha: first, the schism that disrupts the turning of the Wheel of Dharma;
second, the schism that disrupts the formal acts (karmavācanā). Regarding the two robes of a śrāmaṇera: first, the patched antarvāsaka; second, the patched uttarāsaṅga.
There are two kinds of sitting (*sūtra on the Good Vision*): first, sitting cross-legged; second, sitting in a squatting posture.
There are two ways of killing (*Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*): first, doing it oneself; second, instructing another.
Regarding the recitation of the precepts (*Poṣadha*), there are two types of abbreviation: first, abbreviating by taking [only the beginning]; second, abbreviating by omitting [the middle].
There are two kinds of precepts: first, manifest precepts (vijñapti-śīla); second, non-manifest precepts (avijñapti-śīla).
There are two coarse precepts: first, coarse speech; second, praising one's own body.
Due to the distraction of these conditions, there are two [sections]: first, the extraction of the root of the precepts; second, the extraction of the virtuous robes.
The two realms consist of: first, the realm of formal ritual action (*dharmadhātu*);
second, the realm of natural law (*dharmatādhātu*). The two meanings of the *poṣadha* (nirvāṇa) are: first, abiding in pure precepts; second, the increase of merit.
The *varga* has two meanings (according to the *Liaoshu*): first, the meaning of accomplishing the root; second, the meaning of conforming to the root.
There are two kinds of protection for the teacher: first, protection of the Dharma; second, protection of robes and food.
The *Shi chao* has two sections on "Proliferation": first, proliferation of complexity; second, proliferation of confusion.
Regarding the two types of receiving food: first, receiving with the body; second, receiving with the mouth.
Regarding the two types of expulsion: first, those already expelled; second, those who should be expelled.
There are two types of offenses: first, a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and second, a *durbhāṣita* (ill-spoken).
There are two kinds of Saṃgha: first, the Saṃgha for formal acts (*karmasaṃgha*), and second, the Saṃgha for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadhavastusaṃgha*).
There are two times: first, the time for the light meal, and second, the time for the main meal.
The two principles and one profound section: first, the principle of the emptiness of persons; second, the principle of the emptiness of phenomena according to the provisional school.

There are two kinds of ordinary beings who seek to know reality (*mahāsaṃnipāta*): first, those capable of purely maintaining the precepts; second, those who fear the retribution of sins in future lives.
There are two kinds of noble persons who know the matter (*mahāsaṃnipāta*): first, those who have attained the fruit of arhatship; second, those who have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

Regarding the charge that the Buddha committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense, there are two meanings (*vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*): first, [the Buddha is] the world itself, and there is no second [to him]; second, he differs from worldly people such that no one would believe or accept [an accusation against him].

Wearing the patched robe brings two benefits (*Jieshu*): first, it destroys the complete [appearance of a layman] and brings one away from self-attachment; second, it ensures that one is not stripped by kings or thieves.
There are two kinds of secluded places:
first, seclusion by sight, which refers to dust, mist, and darkness; second, seclusion by hearing, which extends even to the distance of ordinary conversation.
I have not heard [of them]. There are two kinds of repentance methods: first, Mahāyāna repentance; second, Hīnayāna repentance (the latter being common to both in terms of phenomena and principle).

There are two kinds of mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*): first, mental factors, referring to all various mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*); second, non-mental factors, referring to past and future form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the Dharma, there are two types of Hinayana teachings: first, the partial Hinayana, which refers to many schools; second, the limited Hinayana, which refers to the Dharmaguptaka school.
Two kinds of kneeling (*Sudarsana*): first, long-kneeling (both knees and the tips of the toes touch the ground); second, mutual-kneeling (the right knee touches the ground).
Two kinds of time (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*): first, *kāla*-time (translated here as "actual time"); second, *samaya*-time (translated here as "conventional time").
There are two kinds of illnesses (according to the *Sudarsana*): first, those caused by evil karma; second, those resulting from the disharmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The disciple performs two tasks: first, repairing the dwellings; second, mending and washing the robes.
There are two kinds of objects: first, sentient beings; second, non-sentient things.
There are two kinds of killing: first, intentional killing; second, accidental killing.
There are two kinds of wounds (*ratnakūṭa*): first, seeking out the faults of others; second, concealing one's own transgressions.
The two poisonous arrows (*ratnakūṭa*): first, delighting in fine robes and alms bowls; second, wrong livelihood for the sake of profit.
The two distracted minds: first, minor distraction; second, major distraction.
The Śikṣamāṇā has two purities: first, the purity of the six dharmas; second, the purity of the mind for two years.
The garbhāvakrānti-purity pertains to the womb. For laypeople, there are two precepts: first, the five precepts; second, the eight precepts.
For those who have left the home life, there are two precepts: first, the ten precepts; second, the full precepts (upasaṃpadā).

The two kinds of attachment (*dvividha-abhiniveśa*): first, attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*), which [the *Jieshu*] attributes to the Satyasiddhi school (based on the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) and the Dharmaguptaka school (based on the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*);

second, deluded attachment (*moha-abhiniveśa*), which [the *Jieshu*] attributes to the schools of Guanding, Yuankang, Hebei, and Jiangnan—all of whom are fundamentally inverted regarding the flavor of the principles.
The two types of *dharmakāya* (*Zizhi*): first, the *dharmakāya* of principle, which is the reality realized; second, the *dharmakāya* of phenomena, which consists of the fivefold virtues.

Regarding the dual maintenance and dual transgression, there are two meanings: first, the single mind whose function pervades all precepts; second, the teaching and practice consist of only twenty [precepts].
Sixth, regarding the precepts:

the two masters establish the substance of the precepts (the *Karmasūtra*): first, the initial master holds that matter and mind constitute the substance; second, the latter master holds that matter and sound constitute the substance.

Two Kinds of Ignorance (*Śīla-śāstra*): First, ignorance that is deluded regarding phenomena, which is countered by the awakening to the three realms; second, ignorance that is deluded regarding principle, which is countered by the awakening to the true nature of dharmas.

Two Meanings of Awakening (*Śīla-śāstra*): First, the meaning of discernment, which is countered by the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the meaning of realization, which is countered by the [obstacle to] objects of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Knowledge of the obstacles. There are two kinds of precepts for *nirvāṇa*: first, the precepts of essential gravity; second, the precepts for avoiding worldly reproach.

There are two kinds of precepts for *nirvāṇa*: first, the precepts received through worldly instruction (the ten wholesome actions); second, the precepts attained through the True Dharma (perfection).
The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* by dividing it into two paths: first, the path of the śrāvaka; second, the path of the bodhisattva.

Regarding the dharma for the fivefold assembly of the two types [of practitioners] (*karmavastu*), there are: first, the five virtues of the *pravāraṇā*; second, the formal motion (*jñapti*) regarding decorum; third, the formal motion for summoning; fourth, the formal motion for notification.

The two types of harmony are: first, that which is called "harmony of principle" (li-he), referring to those from the stage of the first fruit (srotāpanna) onwards; second, that which is called "harmony of phenomena" (shi-he), referring to those from the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana) downwards.
There are two meanings for relinquishing the precepts: first, so that the offense of pārājika is not established; second, so that there is no obstruction to coming and going.
There are two kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth;
second, the gift of the Dharma. There are two kinds of sustenance: first, right livelihood; second, wrong livelihood.
There are two kinds of forest hermitages: first, forest hermitages where there are difficulties; second, forest hermitages where there are no difficulties.
There are two kinds of assemblies: those that can be distinguished and those that cannot be distinguished.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), two persons are established to preside over the proceedings: first, the Master of Dignified Conduct (*īryāpatha-ācārya*), and second, the Preacher of the *Poṣadha* (*śīla-deśaka*). (From the *Shōsō*)

Regarding the two remaining conditions for eating apart from the assembly: first, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states it is due to the time of [receiving] robes; second, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (or *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*) states it is due to the turn of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the two types of *mokṣa*: first, the *mokṣa* of instruction (*anuśāsanā-mokṣa*); second, the *mokṣa* of majestic power (*anubhāva-mokṣa*). (From the *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are two types of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): first, that obtained through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); second, that obtained as the karmic retribution for actions performed in previous lives.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are two kinds of eyes: first, the physical organ (*rūpa-indriya*, referring to the eyes, ears, nose, etc.); second, the ultimate faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*, referring to the aspect of cognitive awareness).
[This concludes the] distinction).
Regarding the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas: first, from the ancient Śākyamuni until the Buddha Śikhin, he encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas;
this is called the first *asaṃkhyeya*. Second, from Śikhin until the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he encountered seventy-six thousand Buddhas.
The second asaṃkhyeya is so named. From the time of Dīpaṃkara until the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he encountered seventy-seven thousand Buddhas;
this is called the third asaṃkhyeya.
The three evil destinies (also called the three paths) are: first, hell; second, hungry ghosts; and third, animals.
The Three Facilitations of Writing (by Shen Xiuwen): First, it is easy to see; second, it is easy to recognize the characters; third, it is easy to recite.

Regarding the matter of non-action, there are three causes and conditions for its removal: first, the destruction of the previous undertaking; second, the death of this person; third, the arising of false views.
The three robes of a bhikṣu are: first, the saṃghāṭī, the upper robe (ranging from nine to twenty-five strips, belonging to the category of outer garments);
second, the uttarāsaṅga, the middle-priced robe (consisting of seven strips); and third, the antarvāsaka, the lower robe (consisting of five strips).

Maitreya will deliver sentient beings in three assemblies: the first assembly will number nine hundred and sixteen *koṭis*, the second assembly nine hundred and forty *koṭis*, and the third assembly nine hundred and twenty *koṭis*.
As for the Three Sovereigns: first, Fuxi; second, Shennong; and third, Huangdi.
The three kings: first, King Yu; second, King Tang of Yin; third, King Wen of Zhou. The three types of wisdom:
first, wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); second, wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

third, wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). The fourfold division of the three wisdoms: first, the cultivation [of the factors]—precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; second, wisdom—the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and so forth; third, vision (*darśana*).
(Attaining the Heavenly Eye and other faculties upon seeing the Four Truths).
Regarding the three Kāśyapas of Nirvāṇa (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, with four including Mahākāśyapa): 1.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; 2. Nadī-Kāśyapa; 3. Gayā-Kāśyapa.
The three types of self-identity view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are: first, the self as a whole; second, the self as a part; and third, the self as a designation.

The three realms (*dhātu*)—also referred to as the three existences (*bhava*)—are: first, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); second, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and third, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The three trainings are: first, the training in ethical discipline; second, the training in meditative concentration;

and third, the training in wisdom. Regarding the disciple’s service to the teacher, there are three meanings (from the *Shichao*): first, to subdue one's own pride; second, to repay kindness through offerings; and third, to protect the Dharma and maintain its continuity.
The Three Meanings of *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Sāmmitīya): First, the Saṃgha; second, rescue; third, superiority.
The Three Meanings of the Robe and Bowl and Receiving Precepts (*Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*): First, for the sake of dignified deportment; second, to inspire faith and reverence in others;
third, to manifest a distinct outward appearance that reveals the excellence of inner virtue.
The three meanings of "not being subject to what has been done" due to prior desires (*sukhābhiprāya*): (1) The meaning of wishing to rescue those in sudden circumstances does not endure for long;

(2) The desire to open up the teachings must necessarily be followed by the establishment of regulations; (3) If the prior circumstances still persist, it may be permissible to transmit [the practice] again.

The *Shisao* (Essentials of the Vinaya) states that there are three reasons why one may not receive a proxy consent (*chanda*) during the formal establishment of a boundary (*sīmābandha*): first, the establishment of a boundary is the fundamental basis for the community’s commonality and thus ought to be strictly regulated;

second, the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*) is weak and cannot sustain formal ritual acts (*karmavācanā*); and third, it serves to make known the limits of the boundary so that the summer retreat (*varṣa*) and other matters may be properly protected.
The three types of practice: (1) collective practice, (2) individual practice, and (3) shared practice.
The three types of uniformity (*jūn*): (1) uniformity of name, (2) uniformity of essence, and (3) ultimate uniformity.

The three types of suffering (arising from the three feelings): (1) the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*): the nature of the five contaminated aggregates is constant oppression, termed "suffering"; furthermore, when associated with painful feeling, it is suffering upon suffering.

Second is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*; that is, when the aspect of pleasure changes, the aspect of suffering arrives). Third is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*; that is, the four characteristics of flux in all contaminated phenomena).
Regarding the avoidance of the three faults when spending the summer retreat (*vassa*) (from the *Shichao*): first, wandering about without purpose obstructs the cultivation of the path;
second, harming living beings deeply violates the spirit of compassion; third, since one's actions are improper, they invite public censure.
The three contemplations are: first, the emptiness of nature; second, the emptiness of characteristics;
and third, consciousness-only. The preface has three expositions: first, the exposition of the single end; second, the exposition of sequence; and third, the exposition of causes.
The three gates of liberation (also called the three emptinesses) are: first, the gate of emptiness; second, the gate of signlessness; and third, the gate of wishlessness.
It forms the gate of liberation.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (the ritual act), there are three interpretations: first, to the point where the text says "binding" (the ancient interpretation); second, to the point where it says "to speak" (*vyākaroti*) (the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*); third, to the point where it says "until the end" (the present interpretation).
In the Mahāyāna, there are the three stages of the virtuous: first, the ten abodes; second, the ten practices; and third, the ten dedications.
Regarding the three points concerning the Dharma: first, not perceiving offenses; second, not repenting for offenses; and third, declaring that desire does not obstruct the Path.
The three lights are: first, the light of the sun; second, the light of the moon; third, the light of the stars.
The three faculties are: first, the faculty of seeing; second, the faculty of hearing; third, the faculty of doubt.

Regarding the three ranks of seats (according to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, those with more than fifty years of seniority are called "venerable elders"): first, from zero years of seniority up to nine years is called the junior seat (*kaniṣṭha-āsana*); second...
Those with ten to nineteen years of seniority are called *madhyama-āsana* (middle-seated); those from twenty to forty-nine years of seniority are called *sthavira* (elder).
The three types of talent are: first, celestial talent; second, terrestrial talent; third, human talent.

Vainly occupying a place among the "Three of High Honor": first, the ruler (whose righteousness is weighty); second, the father (whose benevolence is weighty); third, the teacher (whose righteousness and benevolence are both weighty).
Regarding the three teachers who confer the precepts: first, the Upādhyāya who bestows the precepts; second, the Karmācārya; and third, the Śikṣācārya.
The three periods are: first, the True Dharma; second, the Semblance Dharma; and third, the Final Dharma.

Regarding the three periods of non-action (*wu zuò*): first, non-action at the time of the cause; second, non-action at the time of the fruit; and third, non-action after the fruit. (From the *Ye shu*)
The three seasons for those who have left the household life are as follows: the winter season lasts from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month;

the spring season lasts from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month; and the summer season lasts from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
Regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, there are three stages: first, at the time of entry; second, after having entered; and third, at the time of exit.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, a disciple should inquire after his teacher’s welfare three times each day: first, in the early morning; second, at midday; and third, in the evening.

The four phrases establish three absences: first, the absence of the three matters; second, the absence of the lightness of one matter; third, the absence of the two conditions for origination; and fourth, the absence of the request for instruction.

In the *Śāriputra-vinaya*, there are three determinate matters for bhikṣus regarding the characteristics of the Vinaya: first, the origin; second, the formulation of the precepts; and third, the subsequent application of the precepts.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is taught that there are three conditions for the arising of the practice of giving (*dāna*): first, purity of faith; second, the material object;

and third, the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Regarding the mind, there are three types: first, compassion and reverence (as when giving to the poor and lowly, or to Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas); second, reverence (as when giving to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas);
and third, compassion (as when giving to the poor and lowly, as well as to various animals).
The three colors are: first, blue; second, black; and third, mūlāna (wood-brown).
According to one school, these three colors are: first, visible and resistant; second, invisible and resistant; and third, invisible and non-resistant.
There are three types of ritual procedures for establishing a boundary (*sīmā*): first, the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*); second, the boundary of the precept platform (*śīlākṣetra*);

and third, the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*). There are three types of great boundaries: first, those where persons and the Dharma are shared; second, those where the Dharma and food are shared; and third, those where the Dharma is shared while food is separate.

The three kinds of small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*) are: first, the small boundary for receiving the precepts during times of difficulty; second, the small boundary for the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) during times of difficulty; and third, the small boundary for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) during times of difficulty.
The three kinds of virtues are: first, the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); second, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); and third, the virtue of beneficence (*anugraha-guṇa*).
The three clusters of precepts are: first, the cluster of restraint; second, the cluster of gathering wholesome dharmas; and third, the cluster of gathering sentient beings.
The three clusters that encompass all phenomena are: first, the cluster of form; second, the cluster of mind; and third, the cluster of that which is neither form nor mind.

Three kinds of taking by means of the mind (*Gāthā-śāstra*): (1) taking by forceful seizure; (2) taking by gentle speech; (3) taking back after having given. Three kinds of boundary markers (*Shìcǎo*):
(1) a marker within the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) outside the boundary for the observance of precepts (*śīla-maṇḍala*);
(2) a marker within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) outside the natural boundary; (3) a marker outside the great boundary.
There are three types of precepts: first, the prātimokṣa precepts; second, the precepts associated with meditative concentration (dhyāna-samvara);

and third, the precepts associated with the Path (mārga-samvara). There are three methods for observing the rainy season retreat (varṣā): first, the "early" retreat beginning on the sixteenth day of the fourth month;

second, the "middle" retreat beginning on the twenty-seventh day [of the same month] and ending on the fifteenth day of the fifth month; and third, the "late" retreat beginning on the sixteenth day of the fifth month.

Three kinds of reflection (*saṃcetanā*) (from the *Saṃkṣipta-avavādaka-sūtra*): first, reflection on the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); second, reflection on malice and harm (*vyāpāda-vihiṃsā*); third, reflection on deception (*śāṭhya*).
Three kinds of concordance (*samagrī*): first, that which should come, comes; second, that which should be granted, is granted; third, presence (*saṃmukhībhāva*).
Those who deserve censure do not censure.
There are three types of protection for the realms: first, protecting the Sangha; second, protecting robes; and third, protecting food.
There are three types of bodies: first, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); second, the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya); and third, the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).

There are three types of lifelong observance: first, the observance of the form of medicine; second, the observance of the form of illness; and third, the observance of the form of karmic retribution. Regarding the three types of capacities:

for those of superior capacity, there are the four reliances and so forth; for those of middling capacity, there are the one hundred and one items for the maintenance of the body; and for those of inferior capacity, all items may be permitted for storage.

The three types of speech (*jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*): first, speech from a mind of falsehood (*śīlavipatti*); second, speech from a mind of pride (*dṛṣṭivipatti*, possessed by those training on the path of vision);
third, speech of mere names (possessed by sages alone).
The three types of reliance on the Dharma: first, the method for requesting a teacher (the ritual procedure); second, the method for relying on and dwelling with [the teacher] (the mental attitude);
third, the method for requesting instruction (the mental attitude).
The three types of robes are concluded (from the *Jieshu*): first, the physical substance of the three robes is complete; second, the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the three robes is complete;
third, the common substance of the three robes is complete.
The three types of methods for granting consent (*chanda*): first, granting consent; second, receiving consent; third, declaring consent.
There are three types of mental experience (*citta-vedanā*): first, painful experience; second, pleasant experience; and third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant experience.

There are three types of objects (*vastu*) upon which these experiences act: first, animate objects, such as receiving the precepts or confessing transgressions; second, inanimate objects, such as establishing or dissolving ritual boundaries (*sīmā-bandha/sīmā-vimocana*);
and third, objects that are a combination of both, such as being separated from one's robes or constructing a dwelling.
Regarding the three types of hermaphrodites (*ubhatovyañjanaka*) [as described in the *Sudarsana*]: first, those who can both conceive an embryo themselves and cause another to conceive;
second, those who can only conceive an embryo themselves; and third, those who can only cause another to conceive.
The three types of gold (silver is the same): first, already-refined gold; second, unrefined gold; third, both refined and unrefined gold. The three *dhātus*:
first, the upper *dhātu* from the crown of the head to the heart; second, the middle *dhātu* from the heart to the waist;
third, the lower *dhātu* from the waist to the feet.
The Three Kinds of Pure Meat (*Tri-vidha-śuddha-māṃsa*; *Ekottarika Āgama*): first, not seen; second, not heard; third, not suspected.
The Three Methods of Successive Alms-gathering (*Krama-piṇḍapāta*; *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*): first, going to one house each day;

if food is obtained, one eats; if not, one stops. Second, going successively to seven houses; if food is obtained, one eats; if not, one also stops. Third, [going to] three [houses]... (text fragmentary).
Furthermore, when going from house to house for alms, one should eat until satisfied without limiting the quantity.

There are three methods for a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) to offer food: first, purification by fire (*aggiparicatta*); second, the substance being a distinct medicinal item; and third, offering with the intention of giving.

There are three kinds of remedies for food (*liao shu*): superior food gives rise to greed and causes one to fall into hell; inferior food gives rise to anger and causes one to fall among the hungry ghosts;
and mediocre food gives rise to delusion and causes one to fall among the animals.
There are three methods for a bhikṣu to receive food: first, receiving with the palms turned upward; second, adding a mark of identification; third, dividing the substance.

Regarding the three types of general conditions for all precepts (*Jieshu*): the first is "being a bhikṣu," which distinguishes him from the other three groups of practitioners, even though they may commit the same offense of sexual misconduct.

First, because it is merely a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), there is no extensive regulation; second, because although the extensive regulation has not yet been established, one merely violates the practice of one's vocation;
third, because there is no serious illness, as one is unaware of it oneself and lacks a sense of guilt.
There are three kinds of concealment (*parāvṛtti*): first, concealment of sight; second, concealment of hearing; and third, concealment of both sight and hearing.

In the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, there are three kinds of consciousness: first, true consciousness (*tathatā*); second, manifesting consciousness (also called the *ālayavijñāna*); and third, the consciousness that discriminates objects (also called the *pravṛttivijñāna*).

The two types of teachers and their threefold qualities of conduct: first, they must be ten years of age or older; second, they must possess wisdom; third, they must be able to diligently provide instruction.
The Śikṣamāṇā has three rules of training: first, she trains in the rules for a full Bhikṣuṇī; second, she trains in the six rules; third, she trains in the practice of conduct.
The Dharma: Three Kinds of Distinct Practices for Teacher and Disciple (*Shichao*). 1. When performing any task, one should inform the teacher and gauge its appropriateness. 2.
Receiving the Dharma, which refers to receiving the methods of reciting and chanting the sutras, etc. 3. The method of repaying kindness, such as making inquiries at the three times of day, etc.
In our own school, there are three types of periods for receiving [offerings]: first, the seven-day rule; second, the half-month rule; and third, the one-month rule.

Regarding the three types of monastic property (the precept on misappropriating monastic property): first, property already promised to the Saṃgha; second, property not yet promised to the Saṃgha but intended for the sake of the Saṃgha;
and third, that which has already been given to the Saṃgha—meaning it has already been promised to the Saṃgha and relinquished to the Saṃgha.

In this Vinaya, there are three ways of distributing voting sticks (as described in the *Yeshu* [Commentary on Karma] regarding the three types of evaluation): first, openly; second, in concealment; and third, by whispering into the ear.
According to the *Samantapāsādikā*, there are three ways of stealing the outward form [of ordination]: 1. Stealing only the outward form:

one leaves the household life on one's own without a teacher, does not follow the seniority of the great *saṃgha*, does not receive salutations from others, does not participate in the legal affairs of the *saṃgha*, and does not receive any of the benefits or offerings. 2. Stealing... [text truncated]
Having been ordained by a teacher through formal assembly and received the ten precepts, one goes to another region and claims to have completed ten years of seniority;

one receives salutations in succession, enters the Saṃgha for the Poṣadha and Karman rituals, and accepts gifts from the faithful—those who commit both of these [acts] together are included in the two aforementioned categories.

The *Yejieshu* (Commentary on Karma) sets forth three schools: first, the School of Real Dharmas; second, the School of Provisional Names; and third, the School of the Perfect Teaching. It sets forth three natures:
first, the nature of goodness; second, the nature of evil; and third, the nature of the indeterminate.
Compendium of the Buddha-Dharma (Chapter on Various Essential Practices): 1. *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, one fascicle: it encompasses the entirety of the fundamental roots of all Buddha-dharmas.
2. *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle: it encompasses the entirety of the practices of restraint and maintenance (*śīla*). 3. *Karmavācanā*, one fascicle:
it encompasses the entirety of the methods for performing ritual acts (*karma*).
The three obstacles (also called the three paths): first, the obstacle of afflictions; second, the obstacle of karma;

third, the obstacle of retribution. The three vehicles (alternatively termed the three sages): first, the vehicle of the śrāvaka; second, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha; third, the vehicle of the bodhisattva.

Regarding the three levels of mind for receiving the precepts: the superior mind brings one to the ultimate state of a Great Bodhisattva; the middling mind enables one to guide and instruct Lesser Bodhisattvas;
and the inferior mind consists of not harming the lives of sentient beings and [protecting] those of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding the three states of mind for the summer retreat (*varṣā*): first, for one's own practice; second, for the benefit of others;

third, for the administration of the Three Jewels. Regarding the three Qin princes: first, Han Feng was enfeoffed as the King of Yong; second, Sima Xin was enfeoffed as the King of Sai; third, Dong Yi was enfeoffed as the King of Di.
The three periods of time are: first, the past; second, the present; and third, the future.
The three vows for receiving the precepts are: first, to sever evil; second, to cultivate goodness;

and third, to deliver sentient beings. There are three types of humble robes: first, those humble in cut (because they have been torn and damaged); second, those humble in color (because they are dyed with improper colors); and third, those humble in substance (because they are discarded refuse).
Mencius moved three times: first he lived near a butcher, second near merchants, and third near those who studied.
There are three paths of goodness: first, the Way of Heaven; second, the Way of Humanity; and third, the Way of the Asuras.
The Three Piṭakas: first, the Vinaya-piṭaka; second, the Sūtra-piṭaka; third, the Śāstra-piṭaka.
The Three Clans (Zhuangzi): first, the paternal clan; second, the maternal clan; third, the wife’s clan. The Three Turnings of the Four Noble Truths:
first, the turning that demonstrates the characteristics; second, the turning that exhorts practice; third, the turning that provides corroboration.
When a person’s life comes to an end, the three great elements dissolve in succession (the earth element, being solid and heavy, cannot be dissolved).

When the fire element dissolves, it causes the mind to become agitated and distressed, with the eyes rolling upward and froth at the mouth. When the water element dissolves, the physical form becomes swollen and the sinews and vessels rot away.
When the wind element dissolves, one passes away in an instant, unaware and without perception.
The teachings were subjected to three persecutions: first, during the reign of Helian Bobo, who styled his state the Xia Kingdom; second, during the reign of Emperor Daowu of the Northern Wei;
and third, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.

Regarding the years, there were three [persecuted] months: according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the first was the first month, the second was the fifth month, and the third was the ninth month.
The three "long" items are: first, long robes; second, a long alms bowl;
third, long medicinal provisions. The three Zhangs of the Later Han are: first, Zhang Ling; second, Zhang Lu; third, Zhang Heng. The three realms of suffering are:
first, the realm of blades; second, the realm of blood; third, the realm of fire.

The three times of striking the *gandi* (also called the "three strikes"): first, a single hollow stroke followed by ten strokes; second, gradually becoming more sparse and larger for twenty-seven strokes;
third, the final loud strike of three strokes.
The three fields of merit are: first, the field of respect (the Three Jewels); second, the field of gratitude (parents); and third, the field of compassion (the poor and the sick).
The three paths are: first, the path of seeing (the first fruit); second, the path of cultivation (the second and third fruits); and third, the path of no-more-learning (the fourth fruit).
There are three virtues: first, the Dharma-body; second, Prajñā; and third, liberation.
Food possesses three virtues (nirvāṇa): first, lightness and softness; second, purity and cleanliness; and third, accordance with the Dharma.
The three poisons are: first, the poison of greed; second, the poison of hatred; and third, the poison of delusion.
The five divisions of days are: the first, eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and twenty-third days (of preaching the Dharma); and the thirtieth day (of the *poṣadha*).
It is taught that the *pravāraṇā* ceremony may be held on three days: the fourteenth, the twenty-fifth, and the thirty-sixth [of the lunar month] (*Sifen lü*).

Regarding the meal, it should not exceed three spoonfuls (*Shichao*): the first spoonful severs all evil, the middle spoonful cultivates all goodness, and the final spoonful delivers all sentient beings.

The disciple is subject to three disciplinary penalties: first, the rule of not losing [the precepts]; second, the rule of not losing the invitation; third, the rule of relying on another for residence.

There are three instances when one should not perform prostrations (*Sāhasrika-īryāpatha*): first, when one is in a high place while the senior monk (*sthavira*) is below; second, when the senior monk is...
One who is already seated in front should not pay homage to those seated behind; nor should one pay homage to a lower seat while occupying a higher seat on the throne.
Regarding the three commanderies of Guanzhong: first, Left Fengyi; second, Right Fufeng; and third, Zhongjingzhao.

The Three Preparatory Efforts (*upāya*) (from the *Śīla-śāstra*): First, the distant preparatory effort, such as when one first gives rise to a lustful mind while engaging in sexual intercourse, but has not yet moved body or speech;

second, the intermediate preparatory effort, when one moves the body toward the other and verbally expresses the intent to act; third, the proximate preparatory effort, when one has reached the presence of the person but before physical contact occurs.
The three dharmas for *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture) are: first, the dharma of the Saṃgha; second, the dharma of a group of many persons;

and third, the dharma of face-to-face confession. The three types of retribution are: first, retribution in the present life (to be experienced in this very body); second, retribution in the next birth (to be experienced only in a subsequent life); and third, retribution in later lives (extending beyond the next birth throughout the future).

The Three Jewels of Manifestation: Śākyamuni Buddha as the Jewel of the Buddha; the Dharma Jewel of the dissemination of the True Teaching; and the Saṃgha Jewel of the five Kulañjinas and others. The Three Jewels of Sustenance:

the Jewel of the Buddha in the form of images and stūpas; the Jewel of the Dharma transmitted through paper and silk; and the Jewel of the Saṃgha in the form of the precepts, rituals, and regulations.

Regarding the characteristics of the Sangha Jewel: the realization of the principle through the illumination of the three jewels in one essence is called the Buddha Jewel; the unimpeded harmony with ultimate reality is the Sangha Jewel;
and the essence that transcends names and words is the Dharma Jewel.
The essence of principle—the three jewels and the fivefold dharma-body—is named the Buddha Jewel; the unconditioned principle of cessation is named the Dharma Jewel;
and the merits of the śrāvakas, both those in training and those beyond training, are the Sangha Jewel.

The Three Grades of Ritual Salutation (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*): 1. Prostration with the mouth (referring to verbal greetings and inquiries, termed the "lower salutation"); 2. Bending the knees (referring to kneeling while standing, termed the "middle salutation"); 3.
Touching the head to the ground (referring to the *kai-shou*, termed the "upper salutation").

The Three Grades of People Who Receive and Maintain the Precepts (from the *Shishi Yaolan*): Those of the superior grade are high-ranking disciples who are both able to receive and able to maintain them;
those of the middle grade are individuals whose goodness does not arise spontaneously; those of the inferior grade are petty people who are able to receive them but able to break them.
There are three grades of madmen: those of the superior grade do not remember [the offense] and do not come; those of the middle grade sometimes remember it or come, but sometimes do not;
those of the inferior grade always remember it and always come.

Regarding the three grades of *thullaccaya* (grave offenses): those of the superior grade are expiated by the Saṃgha within the boundary (*sīmā*); those of the middle grade are expiated by four monks outside the boundary; and those of the inferior grade...
One person’s portion.
Regarding the three grades of bowl capacity: the superior bowl is three *dō* (bushels), the middle bowl is two and a half *dō*, and the small bowl is one and a half *dō*.
Regarding the three grades of *yojana*: according to the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the superior grade is eighty *ri*, the middle grade is sixty *ri*, and the inferior grade is forty *ri*.
The bhikṣu has three names based on the causal stage: Destroyer of Māra, Mendicant, and Destroyer of Afflictions. Regarding the three titles based on the resultant stage:
Slayer of Foes, Worthy of Offerings, and One Beyond Birth.
The three names for the Vinaya teachings are: first, *vinaya*, which means "extinction" (*mie*) and is translated as "discipline" (*lü*);
second, *śīla*, which means "precept" (*jie*); and third, *prātimokṣa*, which means "individual liberation" (*biebie jietuo*).
The three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): first, the divine eye; second, the recollection of past lives;
third, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*): first, space (*ākāśa*); second, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*);

third, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). The three types of verbal abuse: first, direct abuse, speaking face-to-face; second, metaphorical abuse, disparaging by means of analogy; third, indirect abuse.
"I am not [the one who may take it], but you are.
Regarding the seven-day medicine, there are three determinations: first, it is correctly for seven days; second, if it is discarded after seven days, it may be given as food to other bhikṣus;
third, if it is discarded before the seven days are up, it is permitted for one's own use.
The single mind has three functions: first, it can recollect; second, it can maintain; and third, it can prevent.

Regarding the essence of the threefold restraint (*trisaṃvara-śīla*) (Nirvāṇa-sūtra Commentary): first, many schools assert it is form (*rūpa*); second, the Mahāsāṃghikas assert it is mind (*citta*); and third, our own school asserts it is neither form nor mind.

The Western Land’s treatises on debate recognize three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*; "direct" meaning manifest and evident); second, inference (*anumāna*; "raising [an example] to show parallel characteristics"); and third, authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*; "the explicit texts of the Tripiṭaka").
These three means of valid cognition establish the standard.
First, the boundary-marker of the realm (*dhātu*) is that upon which the proponent relies; second, the characteristic of the boundary is the ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
That which is enumerated as the essence of the three realms is precisely the basis for the performance of the rite.
The three wheels are: first, the body wheel; second, the speech wheel; and third, the recollection wheel.
The three wheels of the objects of giving are: first, the giver; second, the recipient; and third, the intermediate object.
Master An established three categories of rules for monks and nuns: first, the procedures for offering incense, taking one's seat, reciting the scriptures, and delivering lectures;

second, the daily practice of performing circumambulation at the six periods of the day and the method for chanting when food remains; and third, the methods for the *poṣadha*, assigning duties, and the confession of transgressions.
The Four Āgamas: First, the Ekottarika-āgama (Causes and Effects for Humans and Devas); Second, the Madhyama-āgama (Elucidating Profound Meanings);
Third, the Saṃyukta-āgama (Discerning Dhyāna and Samādhi); Fourth, the Dīrgha-āgama (Refuting Erroneous Views).
The four classes of precepts are: first, the one-day precepts; second, the five precepts; third, the eight precepts; and fourth, the full precepts.

Regarding the calculation for those deficient in years, there are four factors: first, the count of gestation; second, intercalary months; third, leap-years (or repeated years); and fourth, the number of *poṣadha* observances.

The fourfold assembly consists of four types: first, the assembly of four; second, the assembly of five; third, the assembly of ten; and fourth, the assembly of twenty. The four invincible faiths are:
first, faith in the Buddha; second, faith in the Dharma; third, faith in the Sangha; and fourth, faith in the precepts.
1. The *Ṛgveda* (the first of the four Vedas) expounds the rites of fire-worship and repentance; 2.
The *Yajurveda* expounds the rites of giving and sacrificial offerings; 3. The *Atharvaveda* expounds all methods of warfare; 4.
The *Sāmaveda* expounds the knowledge of engaging in battle with foreign nations.

Regarding the two types—the fundamental (mūla) and the derivative (anuvartaka)—there are four distinctions: first, the fundamental is the total abandonment while the derivative is the partial abandonment; second, the fundamental is the root while the derivative is the branch;
third, the fundamental is the preventive restraint while the derivative is the remedial counteractive; fourth, the fundamental is fixed in its degree while the derivative is not fixed.

Regarding the two—*samādāna* (undertaking) and *anuvartana* (following)—there are four differences and one similarity: first, they differ in that the undertaking arises all at once as a general impulse, whereas the following arises gradually as specific instances;

second, they differ in that the undertaking is long because it is intended for a single lifetime, while the following is short because it ceases when the specific matter is concluded; third, they differ in that the undertaking is broad as it encompasses all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), whereas the following is narrow as it is restricted to the nature of goodness (*kuśala-svabhāva*);
fourth, they differ in that the undertaking serves as the root while the following serves as the branches. As for their similarity, both are non-informative (*avijñapti*).
The four reliances establish four types of exceptions to the prohibitions: first, regarding clothing, the exception for robes offered by donors and for robes cut and torn;

second, regarding food, the exception for communal and individual invitations; third, regarding seats, the exception for private rooms and small chambers; and fourth, regarding medicine, the exception for ghee, oil, honey, and so forth.
The Dharma has four reliances: first, rely on the Dharma and not on the person; second, rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not on sūtras of interpretable meaning;
third, rely on the meaning and not on the words; fourth, rely on wisdom and not on consciousness.

Regarding the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) for persons: the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is the first reliance; those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) are the second reliance; those who have attained the second and third fruits (*sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin*) are the third reliance;
and those who have attained the fourth fruit (*arhat*) are the fourth reliance.
The practice of the four reliances consists of: (1) rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*), (2) alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), (3) sitting at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūla*), and (4) decomposed medicines (*pūtimukta*).
The Four Kings fathered eight sons: 1. King Śuddhodana fathered [two]: (1) Siddhārtha and (2) Nanda; 2. King Śuklodana fathered [two]:
(1) Devadatta and (2) Ānanda; 3. King Droṇodana fathered [two]: (1) Mahānāman and (2) Aniruddha; 4. King Amṛtodana fathered [two]:
(1) Bhadrika and (2) Tiṣya, along with a daughter, Amṛtā.
The four objects of gratitude are: first, the king; second, one's parents; third, the teacher and the Saṅgha;
and fourth, the donor. The four great rivers are: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Sindhu; third, the Vakṣu; and fourth, the Sītā.
The four seas (according to the *Erya*): the nine Yi tribes in the east, the eight Di tribes in the north, the seven Rong tribes in the west, and the six Man tribes in the south.
Four offenses involving repeated commission (from the *Jieshu*): 1. Washing robes; 2. Carrying wool; 3. Carding wool; 4. Rainy-season robes. Four offenses concerning admonition: 1.
Causing a schism in the Saṃgha and refusing admonition; 2. Aiding in causing a schism and refusing admonition; 3. Defiling families and being expelled yet slandering [the Saṃgha].
The evil-natured do not accept instruction.
Regarding the four meanings of *vinaya* (according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*): first, the precepts are the level ground of the Buddha-dharma, upon which all myriad virtues grow;
second, all disciples of the Buddha abide by relying on the precepts; third, all sentient beings exist by virtue of the precepts; fourth, [the precepts] are the source from which [all things] arise.
The four [factors] that serve as the initial gateway to *nirvāṇa* are the jeweled ornaments of the Buddha-dharma, capable of adorning the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the difference between the dharmas of "receiving" and "abandoning," there are four meanings (*Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*): 1. Receiving the precepts is like ascending a high mountain; it requires many conditions and much effort.

Abandoning the precepts and retreating from the Path is like falling from a height; therefore, it does not require many conditions. 2. One should not give rise to prior affliction. If one restrains the conditions [for transgression], [the precepts are maintained].

If one says that because there are many afflictions, one must receive many renunciations from many people—what need is there for this? Regarding the three types of renunciation: it is like entering the sea to gather treasures;
if one abandons them, it is like losing wealth to kings, thieves, water, or fire, which may be swept away in an instant. Regarding the four types of renunciation:

they involve the mind’s preliminary acceptance, yet when confronted by external objects, the emotions become urgent. Even if one’s joyful adherence to precepts and conduct is not uniform, and one has already formed the resolve to renounce through speech, one still does not rely upon [the formal rite].
The practice involves many conditions.
Regarding the four objects [of touch], they differ as follows (*Śīla-viniścaya-ṭīkā*): first, a human; second, a non-human; third, an animal; fourth, a wooden stump.
Regarding the four states of contact, they are: first, being awake; second, sleeping; third, recently deceased; fourth, slightly decomposed.
There are four types of obstacles: first, the obstacle of defilement; second, the obstacle of separation; third, the obstacle of sentient beings; and fourth, the obstacle of the realms.

Regarding the four permutations concerning whether a disciple should depart or remain (according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*): first, departing without asking (when there is neither Dharma nor food); second, departing after asking (when there is food but no Dharma);

third, remaining in hardship (when there is Dharma but no food, one should not depart for the duration of one's life); and fourth, remaining in comfort (when there is both food and Dharma, one should not depart even if neglected).

The four distinct categories (from the *Jieshu*): 1. It is a distinct [quorum] but not sufficient; this refers to those who should have come but did not, or those who did not grant their consent (*chanda*).

2. It is sufficient but not distinct; this refers to virtuous bhikṣus whose bodies participate in the assembly. 3. It is both sufficient and distinct; this refers to those who receive censure from others. 4. It is neither distinct nor sufficient;
this refers to those who are sleeping, in meditative absorption, mute, deaf, and so forth.
The four propositions regarding persons and locations (from the *Zichi*): 1. Both the person and the location can be divided; 2. Both the person and the location cannot [be divided];
3. The person can [be divided] but the location cannot; 4. The location can [be divided] but the person cannot. (From the second to the fourth, they gather at sixty-three paces.)
Regarding the failure of the *Poṣadha* (Recitation of Precepts), there are four permutations: first, hearing but not seeing; second, seeing but not hearing; third, both seeing and hearing;
fourth, neither seeing nor hearing.

The offenses of formal discipline (*śīla-karma*) are divided into four permutations (as stated in the *Sānqiānwēi jīng*): first, there are those who commit offenses against the Buddha-dharma that are not [recognized as such by] the world.

Regarding offenses: those such as possessing wealth after the precepts have been established or being separated from one's robe for two days are worldly offenses, not offenses against the Buddha-dharma;

this means that prior to the establishment of the rules, acts such as killing or stealing were both [worldly and dharma offenses]. Those such as committing sexual misconduct or deception after the extensive teachings have been established are neither;
this refers to acts such as killing grasses and trees prior to the establishment of the extensive rules.
1. Question regarding a precept-breaking Upādhyāya: "Do you know that your Upādhyāya has broken the precepts? Answer: "I do not know. [Result: One obtains the precepts. 2. Again, question:
"Do you know that it is improper to receive [the precepts] from this person? Answer: "I do not know. [Result: One obtains the precepts. 3. Again, question:
"Do you know whether you have received [the precepts] from this person or not? Answer: "I do not know. [Result: One obtains the precepts. 4. Question as follows:
The first three questions were all answered with the knowledge that they could not receive the precepts.
The Four Great Vows are: First, innumerable afflictions—I vow to sever them; Second, infinite dharma-gates—I vow to study them;
Third, boundless sentient beings—I vow to deliver them; Fourth, unsurpassed Buddha-way—I vow to accomplish it.

The four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are: first, the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), which relinquishes form and takes space as its object; second, the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), which relinquishes space and takes consciousness as its object;

third, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), in which the mind has nothing whatsoever because it has relinquished the sphere of infinite consciousness; and fourth, the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which relinquishes the perceptions of both extremes.

The four fruits are: first, *srotāpanna* (here translated as "entry into the stream"); second, *sakṛdāgāmin* (here translated as "once-returner"); third, *anāgāmin* (here translated as "non-returner");
and fourth, *arhat* (here translated as "one who is no longer subject to birth").

**The Abandonment of the Four Faults Regarding Food (from the *Vinayavibhaṅga*):** 1. Abandoning the fault of intoxication through food. 2. Abandoning the fault of attachment to pleasure. 3. Abandoning the fault of craving for fine flavors. 4. Abandoning the fault of adorning the body.

**The Tathāgata’s Realization of the Four Faults (from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā*):** 1. Not conforming to the constant dharma of all Buddhas. 2. Contradicting one's own words regarding the governance of discipline.
The Dharma has three aspects that cause sentient beings to feel fear and unease. To speak of others' faults and transgressions in a contrary manner is not the character of a Great Man.

When ordinary persons receive the precepts, they may incur four faults (according to the *Mahīśāsaka-śāstra*): first, delighting in lower realms; second, being susceptible to retreating from the path of the Dharma;
third, being susceptible to changing one's gender; and fourth, severing the roots of goodness through false views.

Regarding the four versions of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: First, those based on the Sanskrit original (where the phrasing and intent diverge from one another, and the terminology has not yet been harmonized); Second, those transcribed in *li* script (which succeed in preserving the essential tenets but fail in distinguishing the specific characteristics);

Third, those sought through interpretive meaning (which can achieve profound insight but have not settled the points of debate); Fourth, those based on contextual circumstances (which appear comprehensive and complete, yet merely preserve individual perspectives).

The four schools establish the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) as follows (from the *Yejieshu*): First, Master Daoyi takes principle (*li*) as the essence; second, Master Huiyuan takes the five conditions (*pañca-pratyaya*) as the essence;
third, the Master of Hebei conversely takes form (*rūpa*) as the provisional essence of the school; fourth, the Master of Jiangnan takes non-form (*arūpa*) as the real essence of the school.

The Fourfold Classification of the Teachings Encompassed by the [Four] Houses (from the *Jieshu*): 1. The Dharma Encompassed by the Three Wheels; 2. The Two Teachings of Transformational Practice and Restrictive Regulation;
3. The Two Teachings of Restriction and Permission; 4. The Two Teachings of Transformation and Restriction.

The *Catuṣkula-karman* (Four-House Ritual) consists of four parts: first, the single independent translation (i.e., the ancient version translated during the Cao Wei dynasty); second, the version based on the Vinaya text (i.e., the version currently used by one school, recited directly according to the original text);

third, the application according to the principles [of the Vinaya] (i.e., that composed by Master Daoguang, which begins with the words "The Tripiṭaka Master..."); and fourth, the citations of circumstances and authorities (i.e., the extensive sub-commentary appended later by Master Huiyuan).
The four *karmavācanā* (formal procedures): first, censure; second, banishment; third, dependence; fourth, prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople.

The four internal firmnesses (*Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*): first, the precepts are not weakened; second, the precepts are not abandoned; third, the faculties do not change; fourth, [the mind remains steadfast].
One does not sever the roots of goodness.
There are four afflictions of a śramaṇa (according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*): first, not abandoning the drinking of alcohol; second, not abandoning sexual desire;
third, not abandoning the holding of gold and silver in one's hands; fourth, not abandoning wrong livelihood for one’s own sustenance.
The four afflictions of the sun and moon (according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*): first, smoke; second, clouds; third, dust; fourth, mist; together with the asuras.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the Buddha has four canine teeth: one tooth is in the palace of Śakra; one tooth is in the kingdom of Gandhāra;
one tooth is in the kingdom of Kaliṅga; and one tooth is in the palace of the Naga King in the ocean.
Of the Blessed One’s four canine teeth, one remains in the world (according to the *Te-p'i ching*); one is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (collected by Śakra);
one was stolen by a rākṣasa (offered to the Southern Mountains); another was also stolen by a rākṣasa; and as for the location of the remaining tooth, it is not specified.
The Fourfold Extensive Exposition of this Vinaya (the *Daśabhāṇavāra* refers to these as the "Four Black Seals"): 1. If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
"Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from the Buddha myself in a certain village. 2. If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
"Venerable sir, I have heard this directly from before the Elder of the Saṃgha in a certain village. 3. If a bhikṣu speaks thus: "Venerable sir, I..."
If a bhikṣu says, "Elder, I have personally heard from a group of many learned bhikṣus in a certain village;
I have received and retained it without forgetting: this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha," then upon hearing such a statement, one should not disparage it.
Regarding doubt as well, one should not rebuke [the speaker], but should carefully determine the words and phrases and investigate them against the Dharma and Vinaya.
If they are found to be contradictory, one should say to that person: "What you have spoken was not spoken by the Buddha; or perhaps the Elder did not carefully examine the Buddha’s words.
You need not recite it hereafter, nor should you teach it to others; it should now be abandoned. If, however, it is consistent with the Dharma and Vinaya...
The respondent should say to him: "This was spoken by the Buddha; you should recite and practice it well, and instruct the bhikṣus and others.
There are four matters for providing support (as increased by four in the original Vinaya): first, food and drink; second, medicine; third, clothing; fourth, whatever else is required.

During the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, one may perform four matters: first, the dissolution of the boundary; second, the re-establishment of the boundary; third, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe; and fourth, the acceptance of bedding and furniture.

To speak erroneously regarding these four matters is as follows: first, to claim that a breach of the precepts has not occurred when it has; second, to claim that a breach of view has not occurred when it has; third, to claim that a breach of conduct... [text fragment] ...has not occurred when it has.
The Ritual Master says that the four violations of the King’s commands do not constitute a violation.
When the Buddha was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked four questions: first, after the Buddha’s passing, upon what should one rely for dwelling;
second, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras; third, after the Buddha’s passing, who should be taken as the teacher.
Fourth, the question of how to discipline Chanda for his harsh speech.

Regarding the four times of eating: (The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra*, according to the *Canon Catalogue*, is suspected of being a spurious scripture and was not included in the canon. First, the meal of the devas at dawn; second, the meal of all Buddhas of the three periods at midday;
third, the meal of animals in the western direction at sunset; fourth, the meal of hungry ghosts at dusk.

The Names of the Four Seasonal Sacrifices (*Erya*): 1. The spring sacrifice is called *ci* (the word *ci* signifies "to eat"). 2. The summer sacrifice is called *yue* (new vegetables can be boiled therein).
3. The autumn sacrifice is called *chang* (tasting the new grain). 4. The winter sacrifice is called *zheng* (presenting various offerings).
