The Auspiciousness of the Four Seasons (*Erya*): Spring is called Qingyang (Clear and Warm Yang); Summer is called Zhuming (Red and Radiant);
Autumn is called Baisang (White and Storing); Winter is called Xuanying (Black and Pure Brilliance).

The four seasonal observances (Saṃghāṭī) of the Śākya school: first, the eighth day of the second month, the time of attaining enlightenment; second, the fifteenth day of the second month, the time of entering parinirvāṇa;
third, the eighth day of the fourth month, the time of descending birth; and fourth, the eighth day of the eighth month, the time of turning the wheel of Dharma.

The four seasons for those living at home (from the *Erya*): first, spring is called the Azure Heaven (*cāngtiān*), because all things appear azure; second, summer is called the Vast Heaven (*hàotiān*), referring to the pervasive heat of the air;

third, autumn is called the Compassionate Heaven (*míntiān*)—*mín* meaning "to pity"—for it pities the withering and falling of all things; fourth, winter is called the Supreme Heaven (*shàngtiān*), meaning that the season is without activity, merely presiding over all from above.
King Yima had four sons: first, Ekacakṣus (One-Face-Light); second, Gajāsya (Elephant-Eater); third, Mārgakarṇa (Road-Finger);

and fourth, Alaṃkāra (Adornment). The four [types of] heterodox practitioners (*tīrthika*) are: first, those who travel in all directions as messengers to seek food and clothing; second, those who look upward at heterodox stars to observe the signs of abundance and depletion;
third, those who engage in various lowly occupations below, such as plowing fields and planting crops; and fourth, [the fourth].
They practice minor incantations and spells with their mouths merely for the sake of seeking profit and sustaining their lives.
They steal from four types of owners: first, the Three Jewels; second, humans; third, non-humans; and fourth, animals.
Non-humans are found across four destinies: first, devas; second, asuras; third, hungry ghosts; and fourth, hell-beings. There are four methods for observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*):
first, the formal announcement to a companion; second, the mental resolve; third, the completion through forgetfulness; and fourth, that which pertains to the boundary (*sīmā*).
There are four kinds of nutriment: first, edible food; second, contact-nutriment; third, volition-nutriment; and fourth, consciousness-nutriment.

There are four kinds of purification of food: first, purification by distribution; second, purification by the donor; third, purification by assignment; and fourth, purification by formal ritual action.

The four kinds of association are: first, providing what is required; second, performing *karmavācanā* (formal acts) together; third, staying overnight together; and fourth, conversing. The four kinds of mutual use are:
first, mutual use among the Three Jewels; second, mutual use within one's own portion; third, mutual use between an image and the Jewel; and fourth, [mutual use with] a single [object].

Regarding the mutual [exchange] of a single object, there are four types of teachers: (1) one who provides the Dharma but does not provide food—such a person one should dwell with; (2) one who provides food but does not provide the Dharma—one should not dwell with such a person;
(3) one who provides both the Dharma and food—one should dwell with such a person; (4) one who provides neither the Dharma nor food—one should not dwell with such a person.

The four types of non-offenses regarding improper contact (*asparśa*) (from the *Shisong lü shanbu suiji jiemo shao*): first, taking hold for the sake of receiving [the object]; second, losing the state of having received it due to external circumstances;
third, taking hold by mistake while observing the precepts; fourth, touching because one has violated the precepts.
The four types of defiling a family (*caturvidha-kulāvadhyāpana*; *Caturvargika-vinaya*): first, defiling a family by means of the household (receiving from one family and giving to another);

second, defiling a family by means of gain (*lābha*) (receiving gains in accordance with the Dharma and giving them to others); third, defiling a family by means of friends and relatives (relying on kings or great ministers to give to others); fourth, defiling a family by means of a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) (taking monastic property and giving it to others).
The Fourfold Delineations (Chapter on Observance and Violation): 1. The delineation of thieves: flattery and wrong livelihood; 2. The delineation of offenses:
fear of falling into the three miserable realms; 3. The delineation of merit: the desire to be born in heaven to experience pleasure; 4. The delineation of the paths: bondage and liberation.
The four kinds of *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: (1) a cloth wrapped around a corpse in a cemetery;

(2) a cloth that was wrapped around a corpse and then brought to be offered to a bhikṣu; (3) a garment without an owner; and (4) a "dust-cloth," meaning discarded items found in streets or cemeteries.

The four names for the year (*Erya*): in the Xia it was called *sui* (taking the meaning of the *xiéngxīng* star completing one circuit); in the Shang it was called *sì* (taking the meaning of the completion of the four seasons);
in the Zhou it was called *nián* (taking the meaning of the ripening of the grain once); in the Tang and Yu it was called *zài* (taking the meaning of things ending and beginning anew).

The four types of persons who commit offenses (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*): first, those lacking shame; second, those who slight the precepts; third, those lacking fear of retribution; and fourth, those who are deluded.

The four types of sexual misconduct (*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*): first, with another’s wife; second, with one’s own wife by improper means (i.e., via the mouth or other orifices); and third, in an improper place.
(Not within the private chamber) there are four improper times (for receiving the precepts): when one is pregnant, when nursing a child, and when observing the eightfold fast.

Regarding the four ways of relinquishing the precepts (*Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*): first, relinquishment through formal ritual; second, relinquishment at the end of life; third, relinquishment through the emergence of both sexual organs; and fourth, relinquishment through the severance of the roots of goodness.
The four kinds of thieving mind (*pañcavargika*): 1. a deceitful mind; 2. a crooked mind; 3. a hateful mind; 4. a fearful mind.

The four kinds of those who should not be saluted (*caturvargika*): 1. one should not salute laypeople or women; 2. one who received the precepts earlier should not salute one who received them later; 3.

one should not salute those subject to the thirteen *antarāyika-dharmas*, those subject to the three types of formal suspension (*tṛtīya-karma*), or those subject to the two types of reconciliation (*dvaya-niḥsaraṇa*); 4. one should not... [salute].
One should pay respect to all who speak words that are not in accordance with the Dharma.
There are four kinds of grave offenses committed through malicious intent: first, a mind turbid with heavy greed, hatred, and delusion; second, lack of faith in the retribution of karma;
third, disregard for the precepts one has received; and fourth, contempt for the Buddha’s words.

The four types of objects belonging to the Buddha (the objects belonging to the Dharma are analogous): first, objects used by the Buddha; second, objects dedicated to the Buddha; third, objects offered to the Buddha;
fourth, objects presented to the Buddha.
There are four types of monastic property: first, permanently fixed property for permanent use; second, permanently fixed property for the ten directions; third, property for immediate distribution;
and fourth, property for immediate distribution for the ten directions.

Regarding the four ways a bhikṣu may consume donated items (*Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*): first, misappropriation, which refers to receiving offerings while violating the precepts; second, [neglecting]... [the text continues with "負"].
The three uses for debt are: not recollecting the gift, and the use for the three types of kinsmen, which refers to the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*). The use for the master is the Arhat.
There are four kinds of precepts (*śīla*): (1) the dharma of the precept, (2) the essence of the precept, (3) the practice of the precept, and (4) the characteristics of the precept.
The four distinct stages of receiving the precepts are: first, appointing a preceptor; second, summoning the śrāmaṇera into the assembly;
third, interrogating him before the assembly; and fourth, receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Regarding the four aspects of observing the precepts (*Karmasūtra*): first, being diligent and not transgressing; second, being able to repent after a transgression; and third, having no intention to violate them.
Holding these four, one may commit transgressions without remorse.
According to the *Vinaya*, there are four types of robes: first, the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) for five days; second, the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) for four days;
third, the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*) for two days; and fourth, the long robe (*atirekacīvara*) for one day.
The Tathāgata has four kinds of stūpas: first, that of renunciation; second, that of attaining enlightenment; third, that of turning the wheel of Dharma; and fourth, that of entering nirvana.

The formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) possesses four factors: first, the presiding dharma; second, the matter to be presided over; third, the person who presides; and fourth, the boundary where the assembly is gathered.
The Fourfold Sequence for Shaving the Hair (from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*): 1. The Elder; 2. One with Long Hair; 3. One Who Has Washed His Head First; 4.
One Who Has a Purpose and Intends to Travel.

Regarding the Construction of a Dwelling by the *Saṃghāṭi*-vinaya (four types of persons for whom the formal authorization has not yet been granted): 1. One who has passed the year [of residence]; 2. One from a different territory (*sīmā*); 3. One who builds a private dwelling.
There are four obstacles and two locations.
In the continent of Jambudvīpa, there are four distinct conditions: first, seeing the Buddha; second, hearing the Dharma; third, leaving the household life; and fourth, attaining the Way.

There are four kinds of dreams (*Sudarśana*): first, dreams due to the disharmony of the four great elements; second, dreams resulting from previous perceptions; third, [dreams caused by] devas and humans...
Because one possesses the four perceptions of the mind within a dream, there is dreaming.
These four continents are: first, Pūrvavideha (translated as "Superior Body"); second, Jambudvīpa (translated as "Superior Gold");
third, Aparagoyānī (translated as "Cattle-Trade"); and fourth, Uttarakuru (translated as "High and Superior").
The fourfold assembly of the clergy and laity consists of: (1) monks, (2) nuns, (3) laymen, and (4) laywomen.

The four aggregates that encompass all phenomena are: (1) the aggregate of form, (2) the aggregate of mind, (3) the aggregate of that which is neither form nor mind, and (4) the aggregate of the unconditioned.

The four types of delusions of the four stages of abiding are: first, the delusions of view within the three realms; second, the delusions of thought (kleshas) in the desire realm; third, the delusions of thought in the form and formless realms; and fourth, the delusions of thought in the formless realm.

According to the *Śīla-sūtra*, the four grave precepts are: first, praising oneself out of greed for profit; second, being stingy and failing to practice giving; and third, harboring anger and resentment.
The *Sifen* (Dharmaguptaka) school does not [include] the four trainings in non-Dharma.
Regarding the sequence of the four grave prohibitions (*catur-guru-dharma*) according to the *Śāriputra Vinaya* (Mahāsāṃghika), as cited in the *Jieshu*:

The first precept was established five years after the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, during the fifth fortnight of the winter season, on the twelfth day after noon, at the time of one and a half shadow-lengths, because Yaśas had committed an offense.
The first precept was established on the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month in this region;

the second precept was established six years later, on the tenth day of the second fortnight of the winter season after the midday meal, at two and a half shadow-lengths [of the gnomon], which corresponds to the tenth day of the ninth month here;
the third precept was established at the same time, on the ninth day of the third fortnight of that same winter season.
The regulation for one and a half shadow-measures before the meal corresponds here to the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month;
the fourth precept of the same year, during the fourth fortnight of winter, at thirteen shadow-measures after the meal,
corresponds here to the thirteenth day of the tenth month.

The establishment of a *sīmā* (boundary for the *Poṣadha* ceremony) involves four locations where the Saṃgha assembles: first, within the *sīmā*; second, in an open space; third, within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*);
and fourth, outside the boundary.
Regarding the four places where a human being may die (*Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*): first, the brain; second, the throat; third, the heart; and fourth, the waist.
The four right efforts (samyak-pradhāna): first, not allowing unarisen evil to arise; second, abandoning evil that has already arisen; third, causing unarisen good to arise;
fourth, increasing good that has already arisen.

The four right absorptions (catvāri samyak-samādhi, i.e., the four dhyāna-factors): the first dhyāna has five factors (1. vitarka, 2. vicāra, 3. prīti, 4. sukha, 5. citta-ekāgratā); the second dhyāna has four factors.
The third dhyāna has five factors: (1) internal purity, (2) joy, (3) bliss, (4) one-pointedness of mind. The fourth dhyāna has four factors:
(1) neither-pain-nor-pleasure, (2) equanimity, (3) mindfulness, (4) one-pointedness of mind.
The four modes of birth are: first, viviparous; second, oviparous; third, moisture-born; and fourth, transformation-born.
In the Western Land (India), there are four castes: first, the Kṣatriya (the royal caste); second, the Brāhmaṇa (the pure practitioners);
third, the Vaiśya (merchants); and fourth, the Śūdra (farmers).

In this land, there are four classes (according to the *Hanshu*): first, the officials (*shi*)—those who have completed their studies and entered government service; second, the farmers (*nong*)—who clear the land and plant grain; third, the artisans (*gong*)—who employ skillful craftsmanship to produce utensils;
and fourth, the merchants (*shang*)—who circulate wealth and trade goods.
The four holy ones established at the altar are: first, the Bodhisattva of the Field of Beans; second, the Bodhisattva Loushi; third, the Bodhisattva Malanya;
and fourth, the Patriarchal Bodhisattva Chengzhao. The four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are:
first, giving (*dāna*); second, kind speech (*priyavāditā*); third, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*); and fourth, cooperation (*samānārthatā*).

The four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) are: first, disputes concerning words (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*); second, disputes concerning investigations (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*); third, disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*);

and fourth, disputes concerning legal matters (*kṛtya-adhikaraṇa*). The four mental factors (*citta-dharma*) are: first, consciousness (*vijñāna*), which means the discernment of the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*); second, perception (*saṃjñā*), which means grasping the characteristics of what is experienced; third, feeling (*vedanā*), which means the experiencing of the objective sphere;
and fourth, formations (*saṃskāra*), which refers to the volitional mind capable of producing a result.
Regarding the four mental states toward a single object: first, a human sees it as water; second, a deva sees it as lapis lazuli;
third, a preta sees it as a river of pus; and fourth, a fish sees it as its dwelling place.

Regarding the four mental states of a father: first, providing instruction and admonition; second, compassionate mindfulness; third, tender affection; and fourth, gathering [the child] through guidance. (Four Sections)
Regarding clothing and food:
the father should maintain four mental states—first, affection; second, reverence and compliance; third, fear of wrongdoing; and fourth, respect.

According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, these four mental states apply universally to the acquisition of the precepts, whether one’s state of mind is (1) wholesome, (2) unwholesome, (3) neutral, or (4) [the aforementioned four].
Mindlessness.
The four mountains press in from all sides (*Nirvāṇa*): first, birth; second, old age; third, illness; fourth, death.

The four dhyānas of the form realm (also called the four great vows): first, the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which can bestow happiness upon others; second, the immeasurable mind of compassion (*karuṇā*).

(1) The immeasurable mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), which is able to uproot the suffering of others; (2) the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which celebrates the attainment of happiness by others; (3) the immeasurable mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is free from hatred and attachment toward others.
Regarding the four characteristics: first, arising (*jāti*); second, duration (*sthiti*); third, change (*anyathātva*); and fourth, cessation (*nirodha*).
The four characteristics of a mealtime (from the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*): first, striking the *ghanṭā*; second, blowing the conch; third, beating the drum; fourth, chanting.
The four characteristics of a room (*sahagāra-śikṣāpada*): first, having a covering above on all four sides; second, being open in front with no walls;
third, although covered, not being complete [on all sides]; fourth, although complete, having openings.

The four phases of transition—each lasting twenty kalpas and collectively termed a *mahākalpa*—are: first, formation (*vivarta*); second, abiding (*sthiti*); third, destruction (*saṃvarta*); and fourth, emptiness (*śūnya*).
Regarding the four characteristics of a village governed by the precept against stealing: first, a surrounding wall; second, a palisade; third, a palisade that does not encircle the walls;
and fourth, a structure with buildings on all four sides.
Regarding the four locations within the natural environment, there are six characteristics for each village (1. distinguishable; 2. indistinguishable; 63 paces).
Second, the araṇya (1. with obstacles: 38 paces and 4 feet 8 inches; 2. without obstacles: 5 li). Third, the path (2 li). Fourth, the water boundary (13 paces).

The four collections (*piṭaka*) are: first, the Vinaya-piṭaka; second, the Sūtra-piṭaka; third, the Śāstra-piṭaka; and fourth, the Miscellaneous Collection (*Kṣudraka-piṭaka*). The Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*;

they are called "truths" because they are examined and found to be real) are: first, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*; its meaning is that of oppression and affliction); second, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*; its meaning is that of gathering and accumulating); third, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*; its meaning is that of cessation and non-conditioned existence);
and fourth, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*; its meaning is that of being able to lead [to liberation]).
The four great elements are: first, earth; second, water; third, fire;
and fourth, wind. The Four Heavenly Kings are: first, Dhṛtarāṣṭra (translated as "Holder of the Nation") in the east;
second, Virūḍhaka ("Increasing") in the south; third, Virūpākṣa ("Varied Vision") in the west; and fourth, Vaiśravaṇa in the north.
The Heavenly King of Śramaṇas (Vaiśravaṇa) [responded] with four answers to the Tathāgata:
first, to abide by means of the four foundations of mindfulness; second, to settle upon "Thus have I heard" and so forth;
third, to take the precepts as one's teacher; and fourth, to govern through the Brahma-penance (*brahmadanda*).
The four virtues of *nirvāṇa* are: first, permanence; second, bliss; third, selfhood; and fourth, purity.
According to the *Erya*, the four great rivers are: first, the Yangtze (Jiang); second, the Yellow River (He); third, the Huai (Zhun); and fourth, the Ji.
The four rules for nuns regarding solitude: first, crossing a river alone; second, entering a village alone; third, staying overnight alone; fourth, traveling behind someone alone.
The four bases of psychic power: first, desire; second, energy; third, mind; fourth, investigation.
Four types of persons should have stupas erected for them: (1) a Wheel-turning King, (2) an Arhat, (3) a Pratyekabuddha, and (4) a Tathāgata.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, four types of persons are taught [to be included]—the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* adds "a manifested person"—namely: (1) the Buddha, (2) a disciple, (3) ... [and so forth].
The four types of sages are the various devas.
The Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness consists of: first, contemplating the body as impure; second, contemplating feelings as suffering; third, contemplating the mind as impermanent;
and fourth, contemplating phenomena as non-self.
The four classes are: first, humans; second, devas; third, nāgas; and fourth, pretas.
Devadatta’s four companions were: first, Samudradatta; second, Khaṇḍadravya; third, Kokālika;
and fourth, Kāṭimodaka.
The four fundamental metaphors are: first, sexual misconduct is likened to cutting off one’s head; second, theft is likened to cutting the heart of a *tāla* tree;
third, killing is likened to the blunting of a needle; and fourth, falsehood is likened to the splitting of a stone.

The Buddha spoke of these for Cunda regarding the four types of *bhikṣus* [attaining] *nirvāṇa*: the first is those who have ultimately reached the Way (those beyond training, *aśaikṣa*); the second is those who demonstrate...
1. The Path (the first, second, and third fruits); 2. Those who receive the Path (the two types of ordinary persons, external and internal); 3. Those who defile the Path (the stage of thinning).

Regarding the four divisions (*caturvarga*), the *Jieshu* states that because these four sections exhaustively convey the characteristics of what is explained, they are called the "Four Divisions. The First Division consists of twenty fascicles (from the Preface to the twentieth fascicle, the Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa).

Divide the alms-food into four portions (*Ratnamegha Sūtra*): first, give one portion to fellow practitioners of the holy life; second, give one to beggars;
third, give one to spirits and deities; fourth, eat one portion yourself.

When Ānanda entered parinirvāṇa, he divided his body into four parts: one was given to King Ajātaśatru, the second to the King of Vaiśālī, the third to the Dragon King Sāgara, and the fourth to Śakra, the Heavenly King.

The Tathāgata possesses four kinds of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*): first, unimpeded eloquence regarding meaning; second, unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma*); third, unimpeded eloquence regarding language (*nirukti*);
and fourth, unimpeded eloquence regarding inspired speech (*pratibhāna*).
The Vinaya has four methods (according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*): first, the root; second, that which follows the root; third, the words of the Dharma-master; and fourth, the application of intent.
Not knowing four dharmas, one must rely on them for as long as one lives (according to the *Mahāsāṃghika*): first, not being well-versed in the Dharma; second, not being well-versed in the Vinaya;
third, being unable to establish oneself; and fourth, being unable to establish others.

One must possess four qualities to be permitted to request formal reliance (*niśraya*): (1) To request that the preceptor take one under his care, thinking, "I shall rely upon him," and to seek his compassionate mindfulness and merciful salvation;
(2) To seek the Dharma of the Path to nourish the spirit, entreating him to provide instruction so that practice may be perfected and wisdom established;

(3) To personally declare one's own intention, saying, "I am able to rely upon you," expressing love and respect as if toward a father; (4) To be able to follow and honor him with reverent service and a sense of shame. (*Shisong lü shanbu suiji jiemo shicao*)
The two dharmas of shame and remorse abide in the mind.
The four dharmas of the ascetic practice (dhūta) of constant sitting and not lying down (*niṣadyā*) are: (1) not harboring anger toward sentient beings;
(2) not allowing sleep to shroud the mind; (3) guiding sentient beings to attain the merit of *āraṇya* (forest dwelling); and (4) [the fourth]. (*Niyatārtharāja-sūtra*)
Day and night, one should not be separated from mindfulness of the Buddha.
There are four māras: first, the māra of the five aggregates; second, the māra of afflictions; third, the māra of devas; and fourth, the māra of death.

Regarding the four full phrases (the four divisions): first, when the quorum is attained, one must not rebuke the four persons performing the *karmavācanā*; second, when the quorum is not attained, one should... [the text is incomplete].
One should not reprove those who receive the precepts if they do not meet the three requirements; one should reprove them if they meet the four requirements.
One should not reprove twenty-eight types of persons.

A virtuous bhikṣu possesses the four fearlessnesses (as cited in *Jiǎnyè sūjì*, fascicle 3, upper): first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of outflows.
The third is the fearlessness in proclaiming the obstacles to the path; the fourth is the fearlessness in proclaiming the path that exhausts suffering.
A bhikṣu has four types of horses (from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*): first, one who is startled and alarmed at the mere sight of the shadow of the whip, following the driver’s intent;
second, one who is only startled after touching the hair; third, one who is only startled after touching the flesh; and fourth, one who only realizes it after the whip has penetrated to the bone.

The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are four benefits to the establishment of the precepts: first, one who has previously committed an offense becomes free from guilt and is relieved of remorse;
second, it extinguishes future unrighteousness so that it does not arise; third, it resolves the net of doubt; and fourth, it possesses ten benefits, such as the gathering of the Saṃgha.

The four medicinal substances are: first, medicines taken at the proper time; second, medicines taken outside the proper time; third, medicines kept for seven days; and fourth, medicines taken for as long as one lives.
The four increasing hells are: first, the Hell of Hot Ashes; second, the Hell of Corpse Excrement; third, the Hell of Sharp Blades; and fourth, the Hell of the Boiling River.
The four Vinayas are: first, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; second, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*; third, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*; and fourth, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

The four wheels (as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*) are: first, relying on a virtuous place; second, relying on virtuous persons; third, making correct vows; and fourth, planting roots of goodness.
Regarding the four types of wheel-turning kings: a golden wheel-turning king governs the four continents; a silver wheel-turning king excludes the northern continent;
a copper wheel-turning king excludes the north and west; and an iron wheel-turning king excludes the east, north, and west.
The Four Floods (*catasra oghāḥ*) (*Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*): First, the flood of desire; second, the flood of existence;
third, the flood of ignorance; fourth, the flood of views. *Lüzōng xīnxué míngjù*, Scroll One. Reprinted by Fùjiā of Sìmíng.
