So that the assembly may collectively codify the precepts, causing those who transgress them to submit their minds; 3. To ensure that all matters are settled through communal harmony, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time; 4. For... [text truncated]

Sūṅ (Senghui) states that this follows the established rules of the Buddha; because the measurements of the various [monastic] assemblies do not exceed [the standard], and because the five dharmas of the Buddhas are naturally so, there is a formal protocol regarding these dharmas.

According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Noble Ones have no five fears: first, the fear of lacking a livelihood; second, the fear of ill repute; third, the fear of death; fourth... [fifth omitted].
The fears of the evil destinies and the five great fears.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—which can also be called the five groups (*pañca-kāya*) as they obscure the supramundane wisdom of true illumination—are: first, form (*rūpa*), which refers to phenomena possessing physical substance and resistance; second, sensation (*vedanā*), which is the experiencing of objects;

third, perception (*saṃjñā*), which is the grasping of the characteristics of experienced objects; fourth, mental formations (*saṃskāra*), which are the volitional activities of the mind that tend toward results; and fifth, consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the discernment of the objects of experience.
In the Vinaya, there are five aggregates and five characteristics: first, form; second, feeling; third, perception; fourth, formations; and fifth, consciousness.
Regarding form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; beautiful or ugly; distant or near.

The five robes of a bhikṣuṇī are: first, the kaṣāya (shoulder-covering robe); second, the saṃkakṣikā (breast-supporting robe); third, the antarvāsaka (inner robe); fourth, the uttarāsaṅga (upper robe);
and fifth, the saṃghāṭī (outer robe).
Regarding the five conditions for the preceptor to bestow the precepts (*Zichi* citation): first, there must be a fully ordained bhikṣu; second, there must be an object of reference.
The four mental states of the mind with intent correspond to the five precepts as they reach their ultimate fulfillment.
Regarding the Mahāyāna ritual for repentance, there are five conditions (*Karmasūtra*): first, inviting the Buddhas of the ten directions; second, reciting sutras and mantras;
third, confessing one's own transgressions; fourth, establishing vows; and fifth, attaining clear realization according to the teachings.

The Five Conditions for the Ritual Repentance of the Hīnayāna (from the *Yejing yishu*): First, the one who repents; second, the object of repentance; third, the mind of repentance; fourth, the corresponding application; fifth, the final completion.

The Five Conditions for Receiving the Fast-day Observance (*upoṣadha*): First, the condition of the field of the Triple Gem; second, the condition of the arising of goodness and the extinguishing of evil through the illness of monastics or laypeople.
There are five conditions based on the three [types of] parents and great ministers; four based on seeking robes and alms bowls; and five based on harmonizing the Saṃgha and protecting the Dharma.

Regarding the five conditions for receiving the precepts (*Karmavācanā-vinaya-śāstra*): First, there are five requirements for the one who receives them: (1) being a human being; (2) having all sense faculties complete; (3) having a pure physical vessel; (4) possessing the outward marks of a renunciant; and (5) having attained at least a portion of the Dharma.

Second, there are seven requirements regarding the counterpart: (1) the boundary (*sīmā*); (2) the Saṃgha; (3) the completion of the required number; (4) the assembly of all members; (5) the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; (6) the presence of necessary requisites; and (7) the time when the Buddha-Dharma exists.
(2) Three [factors] for the formal act of requesting the precepts; (3) the correspondence between the internal mind and the external object; (4) the completion of the ritual action.
Five conditions for retaining the *saṃghāṭī*: (1) fear or suspicion of fear; (2) rain or suspicion that it will rain;
(3) mending the *saṃghāṭī*; (4) washing or dyeing it; (5) storing or lifting it up.

The five conditions for relinquishing the precepts (*śīla*) (from the *Jieshu*): first, being a bhikṣu; second, having a person as the object of address; third, possessing the intention to relinquish;
fourth, the correspondence between the mind and the object; fifth, the completion upon a single utterance.
The five precepts are: first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not lying; and fifth, not drinking intoxicants.

The five hindrances (so named because they can shroud the pure and wholesome mind) are: first, sensual desire (insatiable grasping); second, ill will (fierce anger and resentment); and third, sloth and torpor.

(1) Sleep (*middha*): the dulling and maturing of the mental consciousness is called sleep; when the five sense-faculties obscure the true nature, it is called torpor (*svapna*). (4) Restlessness and Remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*): the movement of thoughts with a deviant mind is called restlessness; the distress and dejection resulting from recollecting past misdeeds is called remorse. (5) Doubt (*vicikitsā*):
a deluded mind that deviates from principle, characterized by hesitation and indecision.
The Five Peaks (as cited in the *Jieshu ji*): First, Mount Tai, the Eastern Peak, in Yanzhou; second, Mount Heng, the Southern Peak, in Hengzhou;
third, Mount Hua, the Western Peak, in Huazhou; fourth, Mount Heng, the Northern Peak, in Henzhou; fifth, Mount Song, the Central Peak, in Luozhou.
The Five Dharmas of Insult (*Ekottarika Āgama*): 1. Long hair; 2. Long nails; 3. Dirty and stained clothing; 4.
Ignorance of the proper time; 5. Excessive talkativeness.
Furthermore, five faults arise: first, one person does not believe; second, they do not accept their teachings; third, others do not delight in seeing them; fourth, they speak falsely;
and fifth, they cause strife between this party and that.

(The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*) lists five meanings of the Vinaya: first, it can produce various supreme benefits, meaning it leads to the arising of mundane and supramundane virtues. Second... [text continues]
1. It can purify the two karmas of body and speech; 2. it can make them upright; 3. it can extinguish karmic obstacles; 4.
it can lead householders to renounce the world and attain the celestial abodes (*devasthāna*), the Brahma abodes (*brahmasthāna*), the noble abodes (*āryasthāna*), and *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
5. it is the practice performed by superior persons, meaning that from Buddhas down to ordinary beings, all act within it.

Precepts have five meanings (*Śīla-pañcārtha*, *Sujāta*): first, they are called "restraints" because they can sever all unwholesome dharmas; second, they are called "constrictive" because their nature does not tolerate evil;
third, they are called "cooling" because they ward off the heat of the afflictions; fourth, they are called "superior" because they lead to the unsurpassed path;
and fifth, they are called "training" because they discipline the wisdom of the sense faculties.
The Five Meanings of Partial Penetration (*Karmasūtra-vṛtti*): 1. To cause Trapuṣa to feel weary of the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is to know that it is not firm and solid. 2.

To cause [beings] to generate the aspiration for the Buddha-way is to know that others are not yet oriented toward it. 3. To summon them as sons of the Buddha is to know that there is no other vehicle (*yāna*). 4.

To relinquish wealth and possessions without regarding them as important is to know that the mind is empty and pervasive. 5. To realize that sensory objects are not the sense organs is to know that consciousness is the true knower.
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Regarding the five meanings of Trapuṣa’s cultivation of merit (from the *Jieshu*): first, for the sake of repaying kindness; second, for the sake of nourishing the Dharma;
third, to eliminate those who practice little yet exalt themselves; fourth, to subdue the arrogant minds of disciples; and fifth, to give rise to meritorious karma for future lives.
The Five Classics of Confucianism: first, the Spring and Autumn Annals; second, the Book of Changes; third, the Book of Documents; fourth, the Book of Rites;
fifth, the Book of Poetry. The Five Elements: first, metal; second, wood; third, water; fourth, fire;
fifth, earth. The Five Heinous Crimes: first, killing one’s father; second, killing one’s mother; third, killing an Arhat; fourth, causing a schism in the Sangha that obstructs the Wheel of Dharma.
The fifth [offense] is shedding the blood of a Buddha.
The five-part *karmavācanā* procedure: (1) "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen" (*kāya-asthi*); (2) "Reciting the root cause twice" (*pratyaya-nimitta*);
(3) "Which elders consent? (*kāya-asthi*); (4) "Reciting the root alone" (*pratyaya-nimitta*); (5) "By silence [you consent]; who does not consent?"

The Proclamation (the skeletal framework): 1. The formal motion in five phrases: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen" (the skeletal framework). 2. Stating the basis by citing both [the offense and the person] (the causal sign).
3. "If the time is right for the Saṃgha" (the skeletal framework). 4. Singly citing the root [offense] (the causal sign). 5. "The proclamation is thus" (the skeletal framework).
Holding the Vinaya yields five merits (*Caturvargika-vinaya*): first, the precept-aggregate becomes firm; second, one skillfully overcomes all adversaries;

third, one possesses fearlessness in making definitive judgments within the assembly; fourth, one is able to resolve the doubts and regrets of others; fifth, one skillfully upholds the Vinaya so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
The five sufferings of eating too much (*Ekottarika Āgama*): first, frequent defecation; second, frequent urination; third, excessive sleepiness;
fourth, physical heaviness that renders one incapable of practicing the path; fifth, many ailments due to indigestion.
The five Kauṇḍinya: (1) Ajñāta-Kauṇḍinya (also called Kauṇḍinya); (2) Aśvajit (also called Aśva);
(3) Mahānāman (also called Mahākauṣṭhila); (4) Bhadrika (also called Bhadriya); and (5) Vāṣpa (also named Daśabala-Kāśyapa).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* lists five types of fruit seeds (*bīja*): (1) those with a hard inner shell (*kapāla-bīja*), such as peaches, apricots, dates, and persimmons; (2) those with a fleshy rind (*tvak-phala-bīja*), such as pears, pomegranates, and crabapples;

(3) those with a woody husk (*kaṭhina-kośa-bīja*), such as walnuts, pomegranates, and chestnuts; (4) those with a fibrous husk (*tūṣa-bīja*), such as pine and cypress seeds; and (5) those with five-fold pods (*pañca-phala-bīja*), such as various wild and cultivated beans.
The Five Faults of Breaking the Precepts (*Caturvargika-vinaya*): 1. Self-harm; 2. Being censured by the wise; 3. The spread of an evil reputation; 4.
Giving rise to regret at the time of death; 5. Falling into the evil realms after death.
The Five Faults to Avoid During the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*) (from the *Shìchāo*): 1. Being too far from a village, making it difficult to obtain necessary requisites; 2.

Being too close to a city or town, which hinders the practice of the path and its cultivation; 3. Abounding in mosquitoes and ants, which cause hardship; 4. Having no person upon whom one can rely; 5. Having no donors of food, drink, or medicinal decoctions.
The five faults of frequently visiting the homes of laypeople (*caturvargika-vinaya*): (1) entering a village without informing a bhikṣu;
(2) sitting among men and women with lustful intent; (3) sitting alone; (4) being in a secluded or concealed place; (5) preaching the Dharma to a woman for more than the permitted limit.

The five faults of preaching the Dharma with a singing voice (*caturvarga*): first, one gives rise to attachment oneself; second, one causes others to give rise to craving; third, one causes others to practice and learn [the manner];
fourth, it causes worldly people to become conceited; fifth, it disturbs the concentrated mind.
There are five faults in not chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks): first, the breath becomes foul; second, one cannot distinguish flavors; third, the heat of the *dhātu*s does not digest;
fourth, one loses the appetite for food; and fifth, the eyes lose their clarity. (From the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*)
The five faults of the transgression of the precepts are: first, having bad dreams; second, not being protected by the devas; third, the mind not entering into the Dharma;
fourth, failing to contemplate the signs of light; and fifth, emitting semen during dreams.

The Five Contemplations on Receiving Alms (*Shichao*): 1. Calculate the amount of labor expended and measure the distance from which the food was brought. 2. Reflect upon one’s own virtue and conduct to determine whether they are complete or deficient, abundant or meager.
3. Guard the mind against manifesting faults by not succumbing to the three poisons. 4. Properly regard the alms as wholesome medicine to alleviate the suffering of the physical body. 5.
Consider that the purpose is to accomplish the path of enlightenment, for worldly rewards are unintended.

The *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) presents five views regarding the essence of the Saṃgha: first, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as real dharmas constitute its essence; second, the provisional function of four persons constitutes its essence;

third, one or many groups of four persons constitute its essence; fourth, merely taking four persons constitutes its essence; fifth, the harmonious functioning of virtuous qualities constitutes its essence.
The Five Ancient Punishments (*Shangshu*): first, branding with ink; second, cutting off the nose; third, cutting off the kneecaps; fourth, castration; fifth, the great execution.

The Five Ancient Punishments (as cited in the *Jieshu*): first, branding the forehead with ink; second, cutting off the nose; third, castration; fourth, cutting off the ears; fifth, amputation of the feet.
Now, the five punishments are: first, the cane; second, the staff; third, penal servitude; fourth, banishment; and fifth, death.
Regarding the five types of *dharmapratyakṣa* (as set forth in the *Kṣudrakavastu*): first, what is the *dharmapratyakṣa* by which the settling of disputes through the Dharma is maintained?
Second, what is the *vinayapratyakṣa* by which the settling of disputes through the Vinaya is maintained? Third, what is the *pudgalapratyakṣa*...
The preliminary discussion on the exchange of views consists of four points. What are the five requirements for the presence of the Saṃgha, such as those who ought to come actually coming?
What is the presence of the boundary (*sīmā*) through the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of proclaiming the limits?

The five eyes are: first, the flesh eye; second, the divine eye; third, the dharma eye; fourth, the wisdom eye; and fifth, the Buddha eye. Regarding the five periods of five hundred years (*Mahāsaṃnipāta*):
first, the period of five hundred years in which liberation is firm; second, the period of five hundred years in which meditative concentration is firm;

third, the period of five hundred years in which the observance of precepts is firm; fourth, the period of five hundred years in which learning is firm; and fifth, [the period of five hundred years in which debate is firm].
For five hundred years, strife will be firmly established.
Regarding males, there are five types of eunuchs: first, those born so; second, those castrated (*kliba*); third, those envious; fourth, those transformed; and fifth, those partial.
Regarding females, there are five types of eunuchs: first, the conch-shaped; second, the protruding; third, the drum-shaped; fourth, the horn-shaped; and fifth, the vein-like.
The five grains are: first, foxtail millet; second, sacrificial millet;

third, beans; fourth, wheat; and fifth, rice. According to the *Wǔgǔ qīngzhòng yí*: first, grain with a single awn (broomcorn millet); second, scattered grain (millet); third, angular grain (various legumes and sesame);
fourth, awned grain (rice and wheat); and fifth, husked grain (hemp and *rén*).

The five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*) are: first, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of diligence; third, the faculty of mindfulness; fourth, the faculty of concentration; and fifth, the faculty of wisdom.
There are five matters for a disciple to attend to a teacher (from the *Li Liufang Jing*): first, one should respect and revere them; second, one should be mindful of their kindness;
third, one should follow all their instructions; fourth, one should reflect upon them without weariness; and fifth, one should praise them from behind.
The five matters for which a disciple is censured for failing to serve (from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*): first, "I now censure you; depart! second, "Do not enter my room";
third, "Do not perform services for me"; fourth, "Do not come to where I am"; fifth, "I will not speak with you."
The Five Benefits of Upholding the Vinaya (Mahāsāṃghika): First, to establish the Buddha-dharma; second, to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time;
third, to avoid harboring doubts or regrets that would necessitate questioning others; fourth, to serve as a refuge for monks and nuns who have committed offenses;
and fifth, to travel and transform beings in various regions without hindrance.
The Five Additional Permissions Granted in Border Regions (*Caturvargika-vinaya*): 1. Ordination by a group of five who uphold the *vinaya*;
2. Wearing heavy leather sandals; 3. Bathing frequently; 4. Spreading out the skins of wild sheep and the like; 5. Possessing extra robes for a full ten days.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that delusion regarding names gives rise to five faults of ignorance concerning phenomena as they follow the text: first, lack of faith; second, retreat from vigor;
third, deceiving others; fourth, slandering the Dharma; and fifth, treating the noble Dharma with contempt.
The five types of misconduct (the net of the Saṃgha): 1. Altering one's usual dignified demeanor and falsely manifesting extraordinary appearances; 2. Speaking of one’s own merits; 3.

Raising one's voice to display authority; 4. Speaking of what one has obtained to agitate others and induce them to give; 5. For the sake of seeking profit, forcibly appropriating the fortunes or misfortunes of others.
Devadatta’s five heterodox practices were: first, begging for food constantly throughout one's entire life; second, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*);
third, sitting in the open air; fourth, not consuming ghee or salt; and fifth, not eating fish or meat.

Regarding the three refuges of the five types [of precepts] (*Mātṛkā-śāstra*): first, the three refuges of turning away from heterodoxy; second, the three refuges of the five precepts; and third, the three refuges of the eight precepts.
Returning to the forty precepts: the three refuges and the fivefold complete precepts.
Regarding the three refuges and the five types of village boundaries (the precept against stealing): first, a single enclosure; second, a wall; third, a palisade; fourth, a fence; fifth, a house.
The five kinds of permissible food are: first, boiled rice; second, parched rice; third, flour; fourth, fish; and fifth, meat. The five ways of receiving ordination are:
first, by "Come, Bhikṣu"; second, by "Three Utterances"; third, by "Breaking the Fetters"; fourth, by the "Eight Respectful Precepts"; and fifth, by *karmavācanā*.
The five types of manufactured implements (regarding their light or heavy status): 1. Iron implements (furnaces, hammers, tongs, anvils, files, etc.); 2.

Earthenware implements (sieves, ropes, bags, spades, pickaxes, etc.); 3. Leather implements (pots, jars, bed frames, handles, knives, scrapers, irons for pressing, etc.); 4. Bamboo implements (knives, saws, etc.); 5.
Wooden implements (axes, saws, hatchets, scrapers, etc.).

There are five kinds of Vinaya masters: first, those who recite the precepts up to thirty-two; second, those who recite the precepts up to ninety-three; third, those who recite the extensive precepts;
fourth, those who recite the precepts of both divisions; and fifth, those who recite the Vinaya of both divisions.
The five kinds of fat (according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*): first, bear fat; second, brown bear fat; third, pig fat; fourth, donkey fat; fifth, fish fat. The five kinds of beds:
first, those with turned legs; second, those with straight legs; third, those with curved legs; fourth, those with inserted crossbars; fifth, those without legs.

The five ways of losing the formal acceptance of food (*Sìshòu shí*): (1) taking hold of it directly without having first accepted it; (2) being contaminated by oily substances or remaining connected to them;
(3) losing the acceptance through natural course; (4) losing the acceptance due to encountering external conditions; (5) losing the acceptance through a deliberate intention to relinquish it.
II. Five Methods of Receiving Food (Karma): 1. Receiving by giving the body to the body; 2. Receiving by giving robes to the robes; 3.
Receiving by bending the elbow and receiving from the elbow; 4. Receiving by giving the vessel to the vessel; 5.

Receiving by placing on the ground and receiving with one hand, receiving by giving hand to hand, receiving by giving hand to object, receiving by giving object to object, and receiving by passing from afar and dropping it.
The five types of ācāryas (according to the *Caturvargika-vinaya*): first, the renunciation ācārya; second, the ordination (*karmavācanā*) ācārya; third, the instruction ācārya;
fourth, the scriptural transmission (*uddeśa*) ācārya; and fifth, the reliance (*niśraya*) ācārya.
There are five kinds of *araṇya*: first, the *araṇya* of the precept against stealing; second, the *araṇya* where one is separated from one’s robes (two *li*);

third, the *araṇya* within the monastic boundary (*sīmā*) where there is danger (fifty-eight paces and four feet eight inches); fourth, the *araṇya* within the monastic boundary where there is no danger (five *li*); and fifth, the *araṇya* of the *tiśaya* [confession].

The five ways in which a bhikṣuṇī receives [ordination] (*karmavācanā*; *Ye shes snying po’i las kyi gzhung ’grel*): first, the eight respects; second, before a community of twenty; third, by sending a messenger; fourth, for one who was young at the time of her previous return [to the lay life];
fifth, the establishment of ten persons in border regions.
The Five Kinds of Non-Loss of the Boundary (*Sīmā*) (from the *Shishi chao*): 1. Release through an illegal and malicious mind; 2. Mutual release between monks and nuns; 3.
Non-release due to being in the center or on the border; 4. Loss of the boundary markers; 5. Vacating the original location.
Five cases where an answer is not required (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*): 1. A preliminary inquiry; 2. When there is no doubt; 3. When one has not committed an offense for which remorse is necessary;
4. When one does not accept the instruction; 5. When it is a formal interrogation.
Five ways of expressing the *chanda* (consent/authorization) (*Chandagrahaṇa-varga*): 1. "I express my consent"; 2. "I give you my consent"; 3. "Express my consent for me."
The manifestation of physical forms has five aspects explained in detail:
the five types of elemental shapes (*dhātuvigraha*)—as described in the *Sudarśana*—are first, square; second, circular; third, drum-shaped; fourth, half-moon shaped; and fifth, triangular.
There are five kinds of medicinal substances (according to the *Vinayavibhaṅga*): first, those measured by time; second, those measured by the watch of the night; third, those measured by seven days;
fourth, those measured by the duration of a lifetime; and fifth, those measured by a general allowance.
The five modes of deportment are: first, exposing one shoulder; second, removing one’s sandals; third, prostrating at the feet;

fourth, kneeling with the right knee on the ground (hùguì); and fifth, joining the palms. In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are five kinds of cultivated plants (the light and heavy protocols regarding them are called the "five types of seeds"):

first, root-seeds (radishes, ginger, taro); second, stem-seeds (also called trunk-seeds: willow, pomegranate, and various vegetables); third, joint-seeds (celery, dock, coriander); fourth, covering-seeds (translated as "miscellaneous seeds": sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and rushes); and fifth, seed-seeds (cumin and cinnamon).

There are five types of measuring cubits: first, the Nan-Wu cubit (short by two *cun* in circumference); second, the Ji-Zhou cubit (fixed at ten *cun*); third, the Tang cubit (increased by two *cun* in circumference);
fourth, the Dong-shan cubit (increased by two *cun* from the Tang); and fifth, the Luo-ke cubit of Luzhou (increased by two *cun* from the Dong-shan).
The five kinds of long-term possessions (*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-mahā-śāstra*): first, precious gems; second, counterfeit gems; third, robes and robe-material (exceeding the prescribed measurements);
fourth, all items that do not meet the prescribed measurements (robes and robe-material); fifth, all grains and rice.
Five kinds of monastic property must not be sold: (1) the monastery itself; (2) dwellings; (3) essential utensils;
(4) fruit-bearing trees; and (5) flowering plants.
Five kinds of improper conduct (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*): (1) physical and verbal intimacy; (2) frequent violation of the five groups of precepts; (3) evil [conduct].

There are four ways in which people act as friends, and five causes for contention and litigation: (1) self-exaltation; (2) coarse and depraved nature; (3) meaningless speech; (4) untimely speech; and (5) not associating with others.
There are five ways to show respect to junior bhikṣus.
There are five kinds of excellence: first, because sentient beings are boundless, the precepts are also boundless; second, because the great earth is boundless, the precepts are also boundless;
third, because grasses and trees are immeasurable, the precepts are also immeasurable; fourth, because the waters of the ocean are boundless, the precepts are also boundless;
fifth, because space is limitless, the precepts are likewise equal thereto.
The Five Rules for Lying Down (Three Thousand Dignified Manners): 1. One should have one's head directed toward the Buddha. 2. One must not lie down while looking at the Buddha.
3. One must not stretch out both legs together. 4. One must not lie facing a wall or lying face down. 5. One must not tuck the knees upward.

The five ways of accepting precious objects constitute an offense involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*). (According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*): 1. Accepting with the hand; 2. Taking with a garment;
3. Taking with a vessel; 4. Saying, "Place it within this"; 5. Saying, "Give this to a pure person (*śuci-pudgala*)."
The five types of conceptualization through which one does not obtain the precepts (*Abhidharmakośa*): (1) regarding a particular sentient being, one thinks, "I shall abstain from killing him," etc.;

(2) regarding a particular part [of the precepts], one thinks, "I am able to maintain this"; (3) regarding a particular place, one thinks, "I am able to maintain the protection there"; (4) regarding a particular time, namely the year, month, and day;
and (5) regarding a particular condition, such as excluding times of battle, etc.
Five Causes for the Rapid Extinction of the True Dharma (*Caturvargika-vinaya*): 1. There is a bhikṣu who does not carefully receive or recite the Vinaya and is prone to forgetting its phrasing;
furthermore, when he teaches others, his text is incomplete and its meaning is deficient. 2.

There is a person of preeminence within the Saṃgha, such as a *sthavira* (elder) revered by the entire country, who frequently fails to maintain the precepts and practices only what is unwholesome; subsequently, others follow and imitate him.
1. There are bhikṣus who abandon the practice of the precepts within the three realms of existence;
though they uphold the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā, they do not instruct either the laity or the monastics, and thus they pass away, causing the Dharma to be extinguished.
2. There are bhikṣus who are difficult to instruct and do not accept wholesome words; other virtuous bhikṣus then abandon them. 3. They revile one another and seek out each other's faults.
Five conditions cause the Dharma to sink: (from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*) first, lack of respect for the Great Teacher; second, lack of veneration; third, lack of humility;
fourth, lack of making offerings; fifth, lack of relying [upon him].
The four types and five modes of theft are: first, taking by force; second, taking through intimidation; third, taking what has been entrusted;
fourth, taking upon seeing an opportunity; and fifth, taking through reliance.
The four types and five modes of the thieving mind are: first, a mind of darkness; second, a perverted mind; third, a crooked and distorted mind; and fourth, a fearful [mind].
A timid mind always harbors the intent to steal from others.

Regarding the five matters in which a teacher instructs a disciple (as found in the *Sūtra on the Six Directions*): first, one should cause them to learn quickly; second, one should cause them to surpass other disciples;
third, one should cause them to know for themselves and never forget; fourth, one should resolve all their doubts; fifth, one should desire that their wisdom surpasses that of the teacher.

The Five Kinds of Unlawful Behavior of a Preceptor Toward Which a Disciple Should Confess and Depart (from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*): 1. My preceptor does not know when I act in accordance with the Dharma; 2.
My preceptor does not know when I do not act in accordance with the Dharma; 3. When I have violated a precept, my preceptor neglects me and fails to instruct or reprove me;
4. When I have not violated a precept, he does not even know it; 5. If I have committed an offense and subsequently confessed it, he still does not know it.
The Five Kinds of Time for the Recitation of the Precepts (*Sīrṣaka*) (from the *Shishi Yaoyong Chao*): 1. The three different days: the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth;
2. Before or after the meal; 3. By day or by night; 4. During the increasing or decreasing [fortnight]; 5. At the proper time (*kāla*) or at an improper time (*akāla*).

The Five Kinds of Merit of the Kāṣāya (from the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*): 1. If one enters my Dharma and, even if they have committed grave offenses or hold wrong views, should they for a single moment show reverence and respect [to the kāṣāya], they will certainly receive a prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles. 2.
If devas, nāgas, humans, or ghosts can respectfully honor even a small portion of this person’s kāṣāya, they shall attain non-retrogression from the Three Vehicles. 3. If there are ghosts...
1. O gods and all people, should you obtain even a fragment of the *kāṣāya* measuring four inches, your food and drink shall be sufficient.

2. If sentient beings are in mutual conflict, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, they will immediately give rise to a heart of compassion. 3. If one is amidst the ranks of battle, by holding even a small portion of this [robe] with reverence and respect, one shall attain liberation.
Five ways to ensure the Dharma remains long after the Parinirvāṇa (*Sudarsana*): (1) The Vinaya is your Great Teacher; (2) even down to five persons who uphold the Vinaya remain in the world;
(3) ten persons in the Middle Kingdom or five in the Borderlands may receive ordination according to the Dharma;

(4) even down to twenty persons may perform the ritual for the removal of offenses according to the Dharma; (5) because of the presence of masters of the Vinaya and those who uphold the Vinaya, the Buddha-Dharma [endures].
He shall remain in the world for five thousand years.
There are five matters that must be openly addressed by casting voting sticks (*śalākā*)—the *Yeyeshu* (Exposition of Karma) refers to these as "examinations":

first, when monks think that among the assembly there are more people who act contrary to the Dharma than those who act according to the Dharma, such as their *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*; second, when monks think that among the assembly there are many who act contrary to the Dharma...
Regarding the case where the *sthaviras* who are wise and learned— upholders of the Dharma, upholders of the Vinaya, and upholders of the Mātṛkā— speak according to the Dharma,
yet the other three groups of bhikṣus do not recognize this and speak much that is contrary to the Dharma; and regarding the case where the *upādhyāyas* and *ācāryas* speak according to the Dharma,

yet the other four groups of bhikṣus do not recognize this as such— in both these cases, the *sthaviras* who are wise and learned, being upholders of the Dharma, the Vinaya, and so forth, should make [the truth] manifest.
When the five types of monks practice these matters, they know that this dispute involves many who speak according to the Dharma and act openly.

In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are two sets of five kinds of fears: first, not cultivating one's own body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, and furthermore, leading others so that they do not cultivate their body, precepts, mind, and wisdom;
second, keeping śrāmaṇeras; third, providing dependence for others; fourth, [providing dependence] for those who are pure.
1. A person living together with śrāmaṇeras who does not know the three characteristics [of the earth]: digging the ground, cutting grass, and pouring water. 2.
Although one recites the Vinaya-piṭaka, the sequence is confused and disordered. 3. One does not cultivate the body, precepts, mind, or wisdom; one lacks aspiration and possesses dull faculties. 4.
One stays in close proximity to bhikṣuṇīs, abandons the precepts, and returns to lay life. 5. One does not understand the profound sūtras and other teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.

1. Because they delight in compassion and affection, they take pleasure in composing verses and adorning their prose with elegant phrasing; because they enjoy worldly dharmas, the True Dharma will quickly perish. 2.
For the sake of food and clothing, they abandon the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) to enter villages. 3. For the sake of food and clothing, they seek much and cause great disturbance.
The Five Names for All Non-manifest (Avijñapti) Following the *Cittavṛtti-śāstra* (*Karmasūtra*): 1. It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it is the antidote to all unwholesome precepts. 2.

It is called "Prātimokṣa restraint" because it is that which brings about entry into the seven assemblies. 3. It is called "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*) because it is the performance of what is wholesome.
4. It is called "action" (*karman*), because action arises from what is performed. 5. It is called "śīla," because it is the cooling [of afflictions].

*La* means "pure and good. In the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, there are five kinds of impurity (each with its own verse; in the *Śīla-vibhaṅga*, under the precept against killing): 1. Impurity of the seed (*bīja-aśubhatā*): This body’s seed is impure;

it is not some other exquisite treasure born from purity, but rather emerges from a foul passage. 2. Impurity of the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna-aśubhatā*): This body is foul and stinking; it is not born from between flowers, nor does it emerge from *campaka* blossoms.

1. Not emerging from the mountain of jewels; 2. The three internal impurities: the substances of earth, water, fire, and wind can transform other things, yet even if one were to empty the ocean to wash this body, it could not be made fragrant or clean;
3. External impurity: various kinds of impure things fill the interior of the body, constantly overflowing and never ceasing, like a leaking bag filled with objects;
4. Ultimate impurity: observing this body with discerning clarity, it will ultimately end in death; it is difficult to restrain, it does not turn back, and it is as ungrateful as a small child.

There are five ways for a bhikṣu to receive ordination (*upasaṃpadā*): first, by "come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*); second, by the destruction of the fetters (*saṃyojana-kṣaya*); third, by the threefold declaration (*tri-vācikā*); fourth, by those who maintain the Vinaya in border regions;
and fifth, by a group of five persons in the central lands, or a group of ten persons in the central lands.
The Five Schools (also known as the Five Divisions or Five Masters): 1. Dharmaguptaka (also called Dharmagupta; translated as *Fazheng*, *Fami*, *Fahu*, etc.
2. Sarvāstivāda (also called Sarvāstivādin; translated as *You*) 3. Mahīśāsaka (translated as *Buzhoyouguan*—not clinging to existence or non-existence in contemplation) 4.

Kāśyapīya (also called Kāśyapī; translated as *Chongkongguan*—contemplation of the double emptiness) 5. Vātsīputrīya (also called Vātsīputra; translated as *Zhuyouxing*—clinging to the existence of the person).

The five types of afflictions (*kleśa*) are: first, the afflictions of the three realms of views; second, the afflictions of the desire realm of thought; third, the afflictions of the form and formless realms of thought;
fourth, the afflictions of the formless realm of thought; and fifth, ignorance (*avidyā*).

The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ascertainment of the Vinaya) cites five types of inducement: first, inducing those living at home to go forth into homelessness; second, inducing them to abide in the celestial realms.
Third, leading them to the Brahma-abodes; fourth, leading them to the noble abodes; fifth, reaching nirvana without remainder.

Regarding the five ways of ripening (the ritual of lightness and heaviness): first, steaming to ripen; second, boiling to ripen; third, roasting to ripen; fourth, broiling to ripen; fifth, frying to ripen.
There are five obstacles for women: first, they cannot become a Brahmā King; second, they cannot become Śakra; third, they cannot become a Māra King;
fourth, they cannot become a Cakravartin King; and fifth, they cannot become a Buddha.

1. It is not the mind; 2. it is verified by five proofs that it is the one mind; 3. it is deliberative cognition, whereas dualistic mind has both clarity and obscurity; 4. it pervades the three natures, whereas dualistic mind has both the extensive and the abbreviated;
5. it is the dharma of retribution, whereas dualistic mind is not.
Non-form (arūpa) is established by five proofs; form (rūpa) is established by one proof: first, form has spatial extension and location; second, form has fourteen or twenty varieties;
third, form is subject to affliction and destruction; fourth, form is characterized by resistance; fifth, form is that which is apprehended by the five consciousnesses.
The Five Constant Virtues of the Confucians are: first, benevolence; second, righteousness; third, ritual propriety; fourth, wisdom;

and fifth, trustworthiness. The Five Vehicles are: first, the vehicle of humans; second, the vehicle of devas; third, the vehicle of śrāvakas; fourth, the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas; and fifth, the vehicle of bodhisattvas.
The five pungent vegetables are: first, onion; second, leek; third, garlic; fourth, shallot; and fifth, *hingukā*.

The five supernormal powers are: first, the power of psychic travel; second, the power of knowing others' minds; third, the divine eye; fourth, the divine ear; and fifth, the power of recollecting past lives.

The five degenerations resulting from violating the precepts (*Madhyama Āgama*): first, failing to acquire wealth; second, even if acquired, its depletion; third, lack of affection and respect from the multitude;
fourth, the spread of an evil reputation; and fifth, falling into hell after death.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that because the five Vinaya masters upheld the Vinaya, the Buddha-dharma remained in the world for five thousand years:

first, for one thousand years, those who attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) appeared; second, for another thousand years, those who became Arhats through the exhaustion of craving (*tṛṣṇākṣaya*) appeared;

third, for another thousand years, those who became Anāgāmins appeared; fourth, for another thousand years, those who became Sakṛdāgāmins appeared; and fifth, for another thousand years, those who became Srotāpannas appeared.

The *Vinayavibhaṅga* (Exegesis on Discipline) enables one to know five aspects—known as "understanding the Vinaya without looking to others' faces": first, the setting of the origin; second, the person involved in the origin;
third, the establishment of the precept; fourth, the analysis of the established precept; and fifth, the definitive judgment of right and wrong.

The five conceptions regarding the loss of robes are: first, the conception of being seized; second, the conception of being lost; third, the conception of being burned; fourth, the conception of being swept away;

and fifth, the conception of being destroyed. The five baskets (piṭakas) are: first, the Dīrgha-āgama; second, the Ekottarika-āgama; third, the Madhyama-āgama; fourth, the Saṃyukta-āgama; and fifth, the Kṣudraka-piṭaka.
The Five Great Monasteries (from the *Śrāvakāvadāna*): 1. Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park; 2. Vulture Peak; 3. Monkey River;
4. Āmra Grove; 5. Bamboo Grove Monastery.
The Five Great Rivers (*Caturvargika-vinaya-śīlanirdeśa-khandhaka*): first, the Ganges; second, the Yamunā; third, the Sarayū;
fourth, the Aciravatī; fifth, the Mahī.

The Five Great Thieves as Seen by the Well-Seen (Explanation of Characteristics): 1. One who does not practice the holy life (*abrahmacarya*) yet claims to practice it while receiving various offerings.
2. An evil bhikṣu who steals the Dharma of virtuous bhikṣus to seek fame, profit, and sustenance. 3. One who slanders the noble ones (*ārya*) and steals the sacred Dharma. 4.
One who uses the heavy property of the Saṃgha to send gifts to laypeople, falsely assuming their approval. 5. One who commits theft.
Regarding monastic property, if one treats it as one's own and gives it away, or takes it from an *araṇya* (hermitage) with a thieving mind, the offense is determined according to its value.
During the late Tang and Five Dynasties periods, there were five rulers: first, Zhu Quanzhong of the Later Liang; second, Li Kueiyong of the Later Tang;
third, Shi Jingtang of the Later Jin; fourth, Liu Zhiyuan of the Later Han; and fifth, Guo Wei of the Later Zhou.

The five *dhūtaguṇas* (ascetic practices): 1. the ten-day robe, 2. the two-month robe, 3. the emergency robe, 4. the extra bowl, and 5. the extra medicine. The five *vibhāvanā* (cessations of the mind): 1.

for those with excessive greed, the cultivation of the meditation on impurity; 2. for those with excessive anger, the cultivation of the meditation on loving-kindness and compassion; 3. for those with excessive... [text fragment]

1. For those who practice breath-counting meditation (*ānāpānasmṛti*) in a scattered manner, there is the contemplation of the four types of delusion (*moha*). 2. For those who cultivate the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are five obstacles.

3. Regarding the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*, also called the five dregs): first, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), during which the [following] four aggregates arise; second, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), consisting of the five sharp fetters (*kleśa*); third, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), consisting of the five dull fetters;

fourth, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), so named because they grasp the retributive fruits of both the sharp and the dull [afflictions]; and fifth, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*), which destroys years and shortens life.
The Five Emperors are: first, Jintian; second, Gaoyang; third, Gaoxin; fourth, Taodang; and fifth, Youyu.
Regarding the two types of "following" (shou-sui), they constitute the five kinds of "sameness": first, sameness of name; second, sameness of meaning;
third, sameness of substance; fourth, sameness of brevity; and fifth, sameness of narrowness.

Regarding the five points of identity between the two types of non-informative action (*avijñapti*)—those arising from undertaking a precept and those arising from following one—their identities are: first, identity of name; second, identity of meaning;
third, identity of substance; fourth, identity of opposition; and fifth, identity of multiple categories.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for the five virtues of a śrāmaṇera: first, having left the household life with a resolute mind because one cherishes the Way; second, disfiguring one's physical appearance.

First, because they wear the Dharma robes; second, because they entrust their bodies and lives to the Three Jewels; third, because they revere and honor the Way; fourth, because they have forever severed affection for kin, being free from partiality toward either side;
and fifth, because they aspire to seek the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering all beings.

The Five Virtues of Sweeping the Ground (*Saṃyuktakṣudrakasūtra*, Chapter on the Hundred Karmic Causes): First, one removes the defilements of one's own mind; second, one also removes the defilements of others;
third, one eliminates arrogance; fourth, one subdues the mind; fifth, one increases merit and attains the arising of goodness.
There are two kinds of the fivefold virtues for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. First, the fivefold virtues of the *pravāraṇā* itself:

(1) being without attachment, (2) being without anger, (3) being without fear, (4) being without delusion, and (5) knowing what constitutes a valid *pravāraṇā* and what does not. Second, the fivefold virtues for the formal accusation (*codanā*):
(1) knowing the proper time and not an improper time; (2) speaking according to reality and not falsely; (3) acting for the benefit [of the accused] and not for their detriment.
One should be gentle and not coarse; one should possess the five kinds of loving-kindness and not harbor ill will.

Regarding the person upon whom one relies for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), they should be endowed with five virtues (as stated in the *Vinayavibhāṣā*): first, causing one to seek what has not been heard; second, causing what has already been heard to become pure;
third, being able to resolve doubts; fourth, being able to bring about thorough understanding; and fifth, removing false views so that right view is attained.

The five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*), which drive the mind and spirit to transmigrate through the three realms: first, greed (*lobha*; insatiable grasping); second, anger (*dveṣa*; violent resentment and hatred); third, ignorance (*avidyā*;

delusion and lack of understanding); fourth, pride (*māna*; self-reliance and disparagement of others); and fifth, doubt (*vicikitsā*; a confused mind that deviates from principle, remaining hesitant and indecisive).

There are five cases where one may mentally entertain thoughts contrary to a formal invitation (*pravāraṇā*): (1) when staying alone, (2) when in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), (3) when traveling a long distance, (4) when suffering from a chronic illness, and (5) when hungry while relying on relatives (according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*).
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the sūtras are spoken by five types of persons: (1) the Buddha, (2) the śrāvakas, (3) disciples, (4) devas, and (5) emanated persons (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*).

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are five ways of receiving the precepts: (1) being born into a family [of practitioners], (2) purchasing them, (3) obtaining them by stealth, (4) having them bestowed by another, and (5) receiving them spontaneously.
"Come. There are five low-caste lineages (according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*): first, Kauṇḍinya; second, Kauśika-Vāśiṣṭha;
third, Kāśyapa; fourth, Ātreya; and fifth, Bhāradvāja."

According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, there are five successive periods of five hundred years each: first, for one hundred years, liberation will be firm; second, for two hundred years, meditative concentration will be firm;
third, for three hundred years, the observance of precepts will be firm; fourth, for four hundred years, extensive learning will be firm;
and fifth, for five hundred years, generosity will be firm.
The five weapons: first, the *ge*; second, the *shu*; third, the *ji*; fourth, the *qiu-mao*; and fifth, the *yi-mao*.
The five diseases of men (*karmavācanā*): first, leprosy; second, carbuncles; third, white leprosy; fourth, consumption; and fifth, insanity.
The five ailments of women (*karmavācanā*): first, having two sexual organs; second, having two orifices joined into one; third, being small; fourth, constantly leaking urine and excrement;
fifth, constantly discharging mucus and saliva.
The five improper foods: first, stalks; second, leaves; third, flowers; fourth, fruits; fifth, finely ground flour-based food.
A single thought of evil can open the gates of the five unwholesome paths (*Buddhacarita Sūtra*): first, a single evil can burn away one’s roots of goodness;
second, from evil one gives rise to further evil; third, one is rebuked by the sages; fourth, one falls away from the fruits of the Path; and fifth, after death, one enters the evil realms.
There are five types of bedding materials: (1) silk from silkworms, (2) black wool, (3) white wool, (4) [wool] less than six years old, and (5) an unsewn sitting mat.
Sweeping the ground where the Buddha dwells yields five merits (*Vimala-prasāda-upāsikā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*): first, one’s own mind becomes pure, and others, upon seeing it, [are likewise inspired].
Furthermore, there are five results: first, the arising of a pure mind; second, being loved by others; third, the joy of the devas' hearts; fourth, the accumulation of karma for physical perfection;
and fifth, rebirth in a good realm at the end of life.
As for the fivefold dharma-body: first, precept; second, concentration; third, wisdom; fourth, liberation; and fifth, the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The five categories of offenses are: first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *pāyattika* (pāyattika); fourth, *pratideśanīya*; and fifth, *duṣkṛta*.
The five primary colors of the cardinal directions are: first, blue; second, yellow; third, red; fourth, white; and fifth, black.
The five intermediate colors are: first, vermilion; second, red; third, purple; fourth, green; fifth, azure.

The five dharmas for entering the assembly (*caturvargika-vinaya*): first, cultivating loving-kindness and compassion for all beings; second, being humble and self-effacing; third, knowing well one’s place in the seating order;
fourth, speaking words of Dharma; fifth, practicing silence upon seeing faults.
The Five Dharmas for Entering a Layperson’s House (*Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*): 1. Speak when entering; 2. Restrain body, speech, and mind; 3.
Maintain a humble and respectful demeanor with a concentrated mind; 4. Withdraw and collect all the sense faculties; 5. Maintain dignified and orderly deportment to give rise to wholesome states.

One should rely [upon a teacher] who possesses five qualities (*Saṃghāṭa*): first, affection; second, respect; third, shame (*hrī*); fourth, dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); and fifth, delight in dwelling [with them].
There are two sets of five qualities for granting reliance (*Ekottarika*): first, saying "Excellent!"; second, saying "Well done!"; and third, saying "Arise! (to depart).
The four phrases are: (1) "to depart," (2) "together with the basis," (3) "if one says it can," (4) "if one says it may," and (5) "if one says it is.
The five phrases are: (1) "to practice well for oneself," and (2) "not to be negligent."
There are five qualities for one who attends to a patient with clothing: first, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not;
second, not loathing the patient’s excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit; third, possessing a heart of compassion rather than seeking clothing;
fourth, being able to manage the medicinal decoctions until death or recovery; and fifth, being able to preach the Dharma to the patient.

*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: "Having received the precepts many years ago, one does not know the five dharmas and thus remains dependent [on a teacher] for as long as life lasts: first, not knowing what constitutes an offense;
second, not knowing what does not constitute an offense; third, not knowing what is light; fourth, not knowing what is heavy; fifth, not reciting the extensive precepts."
Regarding the three thousand modes of dignified conduct for serving a teacher, there are two types of five practices: first, one should go at once to inquire after the health of both teachers;
second, if the teachers call, one must immediately put on the *kāṣāya* and go, never going alone; third, one should sweep the floor, prepare water for washing, and wipe down the beds and mats;

fourth, if there is anything to be done, or when entering, leaving, walking, or staying, one must report it; fifth, upon receiving the scriptures, one should inquire about their meaning until they are understood or not.

One should not harbor fear; first, one should go there repeatedly; second, upon reaching the door, one should snap the fingers three times; third, upon entering, one should prostrate with the head and face touching the ground;
fourth, one should kneel long and inquire after their well-being; fifth, one should turn back toward the door before departing.
The Two Sets of Five Dharmas for Acting as a Teacher to Laypeople (*Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*): 1. Not being an old acquaintance, one does not socialize with them. 2.
One does not seek to use one's influence to manage the household affairs of the *dānapati*. 3. One does not converse in secret with them, thereby causing suspicion to arise within the family. 4.
One does not instruct them on auspicious times or dates for performing sacrifices to spirits and deities. 5. One does not exceed the limits of what they request.
1. One should not reside in the house of a donor; 2. one should not fix the mind on greed for profit; 3. one should preach the Dharma to individuals separately;
4. one should not engage in shared entertainment; 5. one should not desire to see [the donor] constantly.
According to the *Mātṛkā*, a person capable of admonishing others need not accept five qualities: first, a lack of shame and remorse; second, a lack of extensive learning;
third, constantly seeking out the faults of others; fourth, delighting in strife and contention; and fifth, desiring to abandon the Path.

The five treasures of the world are difficult to obtain (*Caturvargika*): first, the appearance of a Buddha in the world; second, hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma; third, understanding it upon hearing it;
fourth, practicing in accordance with the Dharma; and fifth, attaining a mind of faith and joy.

The five reasons for translating [terms] from the Sanskrit language (from the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*): first, because they are esoteric; second, because they possess multiple meanings; third, because they do not exist in this land;
fourth, to conform with antiquity; and fifth, to engender wholesome roots.
The five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*) are so called because: (1) there is no interval in their destination, as one is reborn immediately after casting off the present body;

(2) there is no interval in the experience of suffering, as there is no pleasure within that state; (3) there is no interval in time, as it is fixed for exactly one *kalpa*; (4) there is no interval in life, as it is not interrupted therein;
and (5) there is no interval in form, as [the hell beings] completely fill [the space].

In the age of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), there are five signs of the decline of the Dharma (*dharmavyasana*; *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*): first, a bhikṣu who has attained only slight realization immediately claims to be an arhat;
second, laypeople are reborn in heaven while renunciants fall into hell; third, some people abandon worldly occupations to become renunciants but then break their precepts;
fourth, many who have broken the precepts receive assistance from others; fifth, even arhats are beaten and reviled.

The Five Benefits of Walking Meditation (*caṅkrama*) (from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*): 1. Ability to travel long distances; 2. Capacity for contemplation; 3. Few illnesses; 4. Digestion of food and drink; 5.
Attainment of long-term stability in meditative concentration.

The Five Medicines of Ancient Sages Corresponding to the Five Categories of Offenses (from the *Zichi*): 1. Expiation and banishment (*parivāsa*); 2. Monastic ritual confession; 3. Confession before another person (*pratideśanīya*).

It is taught that there are four types of confession before another person (*pratideśanīya*), one type of confession with a single recitation, five types of remorseful confession within one's own mind, and five parables from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding a rākṣasa begging for a life-preserving bag: (1) begging for the whole bag represents the commission of the four *pārājika* offenses;

(2) begging for half and being granted it represents the commission of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; (3) begging for a small amount represents the commission of a *sthūlātyaya* offense; and (4) begging for the measure of a finger represents the commission of a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Tiṣya’s five [sins] are likened to the size of motes of dust; they constitute minor offenses (duṣkṛta).

The five desires (also called the five objects of sensory dust) are: first, the desire for forms; second, the desire for sounds; third, the desire for fragrances; fourth, the desire for tastes; and fifth, the desire for tactile sensations.

The five sharp fetters (*pañca tīkṣṇa-āsava*; *āsrava* is defined as "driving and enjoining"): 1. The view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*): falsely calculating [the five aggregates] to be a self. 2. The view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*): mutually adhering to one extreme; in total, there are sixty-two such views. 3. Wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*):

denying cause and effect, thereby severing the roots of goodness. 4. Adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): erroneously taking what is not a true precept to be a precept. 5. Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*):
erroneously calculating what is not the Dharma to give rise to a mind that clings to it.

The Five Benefits of the Summer Retreat (*Varṣā*) (from the *Shìchão*): 1. Possessing surplus wealth; 2. Staying overnight apart from one’s robes; 3. Accepting invitations while facing away [from the monastery];
4. Eating separately from the community; 5. Visiting other households before or after a meal.

The Five Benefits of the Buddha’s Visiting the Quarters (*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*): First, my disciples will not be attached to conditioned affairs; second, they will not be attached to worldly discourse;
third, they will not be attached to sleep which obstructs the practice of the Path; fourth, they shall visit those who are ill;
fifth, young novices who see the Buddha’s majestic demeanor will give rise to a heart of joy.
The five powers are: first, the power of faith; second, the power of diligence; third, the power of mindfulness; fourth, the power of concentration; and fifth, the power of wisdom.

Regarding the *Zizhi*, there are five sections: first, establishing the fundamental principle; second, distinguishing the teachings; third, recording citations; fourth, clarifying refutations and proofs; and fifth, indicating omissions and doubts.
The six categories of ordination through *karmavācanā* are: first, ten persons in the central regions; second, five persons in the borderlands; third, twenty persons among the nuns;
fourth, ten persons established by principle among the nuns; fifth, those of young age who have previously been married; and sixth, those sent by messenger.

The Six Conditions for Receiving Offerings (*Sīruǎn shìchāo*): First, the Buddha; second, the Dharma; third, the Sangha; fourth, the stupa; fifth, those nursing the sick; sixth, the sick person. The Six Meanings of Taking Refuge in the Triple Gem (*Jièshū*):
First, gratitude for their kindness; second, receiving their protection; third, generating faith; fourth, expressing reverence; fifth, manifesting excellence;
sixth, opening the way for sentient beings to contemplate the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The Jewel has six meanings (*Ratnagotravibhāga*): 1. The meaning of rarity: Worldly jewels are absent for those who are impoverished; the Three Jewels are not encountered by those lacking merit.

2. The meaning of being free from defilement: Worldly jewels have no physical blemishes; the Three Jewels are utterly free from all outflows (*āsrava*). 3. The meaning of power: Worldly jewels remove poverty and eliminate poison;
the Three Jewels possess the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) that are inconceivable. 4. The meaning of adornment... [text continues]
The meaning of the world’s jewel-adorned body making it beautiful: the Three Jewels can adorn the Dharma-body.

Among all things, the Three Jewels are the most excellent of the five supreme worldly jewels; they are unsurpassed among all that exists. The meaning of the six unchanging worldly jewels: they are refined and polished yet remain immutable;
the Three Jewels are unmoved by the eight worldly winds.

The Odes have six meanings (from the Preface to the Mao Shih): first, *feng* (to satirize the superior so as to transform the subordinate); second, *fu* (to set forth the meaning); third, *bi* (to take up the meaning through comparison);
fourth, *xing* (to be moved by things); fifth, *ya* (matters of government and administration); sixth, *song* (the accomplishment of success).
The Six Classics of the Confucian tradition: first, the Spring and Autumn Annals; second, the Book of Changes; third, the Book of Documents;
fourth, the Book of Poetry; fifth, the Book of Rites; sixth, the Record of Music. The Six Groups of Bhikṣus (from the *Jieshu*): first, Nantuo; second, Upananda;
third, Kālodāyin; fourth, Channa; fifth, Māṭhara; sixth, Pūrṇa.
The six faults of associating with evil persons (*Zishi*: *Zichichi*). First, the destruction of one's reputation; second, the obstruction of the path of study;
third, the loss of virtuous conduct; fourth, the loss of right faith; fifth, the severing of the roots of goodness; sixth, falling into the evil realms.
Among worldly matters, the six arts are: first, ritual; second, music; third, archery; fourth, charioteering; fifth, calligraphy; and sixth, mathematics.
The six faculties are: first, the eye; second, the ear; third, the nose; fourth, the tongue; fifth, the body; and sixth, the mind.
The Six States: 1. Han, 2. Wei, 3. Yan, 4. Zhao, 5. Qi, 6. Chu.
The Six Days of Fasting (*Jizulun*): 1. The eighth day (the celestial king’s messenger descends); 2. The twenty-fourth day (the celestial king’s crown prince descends);
3. The fifteenth day (the celestial king himself descends); 4. The twenty-third day (the celestial king’s messenger descends); 5. The twenty-ninth day (the celestial king...).
The Crown Prince descended. Sixty days (the Heavenly King descended himself).
The Six Masters who upheld the Vinaya (*Shichao*): 1. They adhered exclusively to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* alone and did not employ other schools; 2.

When there were missing texts in their own school, they took passages from external sources for citation; 3. Where there was only the meaning but no text in their own school, they took passages from external sources for citation; 4. This school...
Its textual meaning is fully elucidated; it is that which other schools have discarded. Fifth, it comprehensively adopts the five *piṭakas* and unifies them with the Vinaya school.
Sixth, it is the ultimate destination and the supreme pinnacle of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the six heterodox teachers (*ṣaṭ-tīrthika-ācārya*) [in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*]: first, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa; second, Maskarī Gośālīputra.
1. Ajita Keśakambala; 2. Kakuda Kātyāyana; 3. Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra; 4. Ajita Keśakambala;
5. Kakuda Kātyāyana; 6. Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
The six consciousnesses are: first, the eye; second, the ear; third, the nose; fourth, the tongue; fifth, the body; and sixth, the mind.

Regarding the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*) in the Dharma-characteristics school (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*), they are: first, *karmadhāraya* (appositional); second, *tatpuruṣa* (dependent); third, *dvandva* (coordinative); fourth, *bahuvrīhi* (possessive); fifth, *avyayībhāva* (indeclinable); and sixth, *śeṣa* (residual).
The six destinies (also called the six paths): first, gods; second, humans; third, asuras; fourth, hell-beings; fifth, hungry ghosts; sixth, animals.
The six factors of accomplishment: first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the principal [teacher]; fifth, place; sixth, the assembly.

The six kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are: first, the power of the physical realm (*ṛddhi-vidhi*); second, knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*); third, the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*); fourth, the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*); fifth, recollection of past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti*); and sixth, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).

sixth, harmony in benefit through equal distribution. The seven factors of enlightenment are: first, investigation of dharmas; second, vigor; third, joy; fourth, tranquility; fifth, equanimity; sixth, concentration; seventh, mindfulness.

At the time of Ānanda’s compilation of the teachings (the Council of Five Hundred), he confessed seven offenses of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*): 1. It was improper that within the Buddha-dharma, he first requested the ordination of bhikṣuṇīs; 2.
When the World-Honored One thrice invited him to serve as an attendant for offerings, he did not do so; 3.

It was improper that while sewing the *saṃghāṭī* robe for the Buddha, he stepped upon it with his feet; 4. When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he failed to inform him three times [of his impending departure].
1. Requesting the five World-Honored Ones to remain in the world. 2. Not giving water when asked for it. 3. The six Tathāgatas not inquiring about minor precepts while remaining in the world.

The Seven Sages of the Hīnayāna: 1. **Five Stations of Mindfulness** (*pañca-smṛtyupasthāna*): - For those with much greed: impurity (*aśubha*). - For those with much anger: loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*). - For those with much distraction: counting the breath (*ānāpāna*). - For those with much ignorance: causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). - For those with many obstacles:

mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). - Two types of specific recollection: 1. Recollection of the mind as impermanent (*anitya*), phenomena as selfless (*anātman*), and the body as impure (*aśuci*). 2. Recollection that feeling is suffering (*duḥkha*). 2. **Heat** (*ūṣmagata*): Like a person drilling for fire, there is first heat and later fire;

it causes one to cultivate the preliminary signs already obtained on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). 3. **Summit** (*mūrdhan*): Situated between Heat and Patience; like the peak of a mountain, or alternatively, like the crown of a person’s head. 4. **Patience** (*kṣānti*): These roots of goodness are definitive and no longer subject to regression or movement. 5. **Supreme Worldly Dharmas** (*laukikāgradharma*).

The sevenfold karma consists of: first, sexual misconduct; second, theft; third, killing; fourth, false speech; fifth, frivolous speech; sixth, divisive speech; and seventh, harsh speech.

Furthermore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are seven disadvantages to lighting fires: first, it impairs the eyes; second, it impairs the complexion; third, it causes the body to become emaciated; and fourth, it causes the robes to become soiled.

The seven kinds of robes that do not require the ritual of *viśuddhi-dāna* (the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*): first, the *saṃghāṭī*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*;

it is called *śīla* because *śīla* has the meaning of purity and goodness.

fifth, cooking indoors is an *dukkaṭa*; sixth, cooking for oneself is an *dukkaṭa*; and seventh, handling food improperly is an *dukkaṭa*.
The seven factors for maintaining or violating [the precepts] are common to all and consist of: first, being one of the five groups of renunciants; second, clearly recognizing the person as a bhikṣu;

third, having a deliberate intention directed toward the object; fourth, the absence of life-threatening danger; fifth, the absence of danger to the holy life (brahmacarya); sixth, addressing the object according to its actual nature; and seventh, proceeding toward the ultimate fruit.

fifth, śikṣamāṇā; sixth, bhikṣuṇī; seventh, bhikṣu.
The seven places touched by the wind of speech (*vāyu-spraṣṭavya*) are: (1) the tongue, (2) the gums, (3) the teeth, (4) the shoulders, (5) the palate, (6) the throat, and (7) the chest.
Regarding the four types of intimacy, there are seven mental states: (1) performing what is difficult to do, (2) giving what is difficult to give, and (3) enduring what is difficult to endure.
1. Being able to perform the four secret services; 2. Mutual communication; 3. Mutual concealment of faults; 4. Not abandoning one another in times of suffering;

The body has six [types of] children and seven [types of] grandchildren.

and (7) the restraint concomitant with the path. (From the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*).

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in Seven Sections (*Tianqin Niepan Lun*): 1. The Section on the Miraculous Powers of Manifestation; 2.

The Seven Methods for Properly Attending to a Teacher: 1. If too far away, one may not hear [the teacher's instructions].

2. If too close, one may step on the teacher’s shadow. 3. If upwind, one may cause foul odors to waft toward the teacher. 4. If at a high place, it may lead to the development of arrogance. 5. If directly in front, it may obstruct the teacher’s view. 6.
If directly behind, it may be difficult to turn around and respond when called. 7. One should stand at a distance of ten feet.

The seven treasures (*saptaratna*) (according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*): first, gold; second, silver; third, *maṇi* (also called *vaiḍūrya*, the treasure of Mount Sumeru); fourth, coral (also called *sphatika*, which is crystal);
fifth, *śaṅkha* (a treasure with an intermingled blue-and-white color); sixth, *musāragalva* (its color is like that of a horse’s gallstone); seventh, red pearl (*lohitamuktikā*;
the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states it is produced by red insects, or alternatively, that its substance is naturally red).

The Sevenfold Categories of Loving-kindness (*Nirvāṇa Sūtra*): **Three Categories of Relatives:** - *Superior relatives*: teachers, monks, and parents. - *Intermediate relatives*: brothers, sisters, and fellow students. - *Inferior relatives*:

those who have bestowed wealth upon me, friends, and so forth. **Three Categories of Enemies:** - *Superior enemies*: those who have taken the lives of my parents, and so forth. - *Intermediate enemies*: those who have taken the lives of my brothers or stolen my wealth. - *Inferior enemies*: those who have taken the lives of my friends, and so forth.
**One Category of Neither Enemy Nor Relative:** This constitutes a single category.

fourth, like a king’s only son whom he cherishes for his succession to the throne; fifth, like a person’s single eye, which they love with great intensity; and sixth, like a poor man in this world.

it is like a sick person obtaining excellent medicine.

sixth, free from error; seventh, deep and far-reaching; eighth, inexhaustible. The eight precepts are:
first, abstaining from killing; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct; fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from drinking intoxicants.
