eighth, not eating at improper times.
Regarding the eight cold hells (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*): first, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda; third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Hahava...
[The eight types of precious lotuses are: 1. *Pāṇḍarā*, 2. *Pāṇḍarottarā*, 3. *Utpala*, 4. *Padma*, 5. *Puṣkara*, 6. *Utpalottara*, 7. *Puṇḍarīka*, 8. *Mahāpuṇḍarīka*.

The ocean possesses eight extraordinary qualities (*caturvidha-āścarya-dharma*): 1. it enters gradually and deepens gradually; 2. its tides do not exceed their limits; 3. it does not harbor corpses overnight; 4.
when the four rivers converge there, they lose their original names; 5. although ten thousand streams all flow back to it, [it remains undisturbed]. (From the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*)
1. Increasing and decreasing [in size]; 2. Producing various rare treasures; 3. The dwelling place of beings with seven large bodies; 4. All having the same salty taste.
For bhikṣuṇīs, there are the eight rules of respect: 1. A bhikṣuṇī of even a hundred years' standing must pay homage at the feet of a newly ordained bhikṣu;
2. She must not revile or slander a bhikṣu; 3. She must not expose the faults or proclaim the transgressions of a bhikṣu; 4. She receives [instruction] from the Saṃgha.

1. Observing the five precepts; 2. Being cleared of offenses through the Saṃgha; 3. Seeking instruction every half-month; 4. Observing the rains retreat in dependence upon the Saṃgha; 5. Performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in dependence upon the Saṃgha.
One who breaks the precepts yet maintains the observance of them and performs prostrations incurs eight minor transgressions (*ratnarāśi-sūtra*): 1. being foolish; 2. being mute of speech.
1. To be mute; 2. to have an ugly countenance; 3. to have a face that is crooked and distorted, causing those who see it to mock and laugh;
4. to subsequently receive a female body as a poor servant; 5. to have a physique that is emaciated and weak, resulting in a shortened lifespan;
6. to be disrespected by others and constantly bear an evil reputation; 7. to fail to encounter the era of a Buddha.
Water possesses eight meritorious qualities: first, it is pure; second, it is odorless; third, it is light; fourth, it is cool; fifth, it is soft;
sixth, it is delicious; seventh, it is temperate when drunk; and eighth, it causes no affliction after drinking.

The eight sufferings are: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from the beloved; sixth, the suffering of encountering the hated;
seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and eighth, the suffering of the proliferation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The eight vows of Visākhā Mother were: first, to provide food for visiting bhikṣus; second, to provide food for bhikṣus traveling from afar; third, to provide food for sick bhikṣus;
fourth, to provide medicine according to their illnesses; fifth, to provide food for those nursing the sick;
sixth, to provide rice gruel; seventh, to provide rain-cloaks for the bhikṣus; and eighth, to provide rain-cloaks for the bhikṣuṇīs.
The eight liberations are: first, possessing internal perception of form while perceiving external forms; second, lacking internal perception of form while perceiving external forms;
third, realizing the purity of the body through direct experience; fourth, the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the sphere of nothingness;
seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and eighth, the cessation of sensation and perception.
The Eight Grounds for the Loss of the *guṇavat-cīvara* (according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*): 1. Simultaneous completion; 2. Loss of the robe; 3. Hearing of the loss; 4.

Departing to a distant place; 5. Severance of hope; 6. The robe exiting the boundary; 7. The person exiting the boundary; 8. Relinquishment through the formal motion and second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
The Master, according to eight criteria, may permit the disciple to go abroad (*Shizi pian*): (1) the companion is suitable but the location is not;

(2) the location is suitable but the companion is not; (3) the matter is suitable but the companion is not; (4) the companion and location are suitable but the matter is not; (5) the companion and matter are suitable but the location is not;

(6) the matter and location are suitable but the companion is not; (7) the matter, location, and companion are all unsuitable (in these cases above, going is not permitted); (8) the matter is suitable.
Regarding the place, the companions, and the act itself—all these must be observed (the word "listen" [聽] here indicates that they must be avoided).
The eight exceptions permitted during times of scarcity are: (1) storing food indoors; (2) cooking indoors; (3) cooking for oneself; (4) receiving food from one who has handled it improperly;

(5) food belonging to the Saṃgha; (6) food belonging to a layperson; (7) wild fruits; and (8) land-grown fruits. (For items five through eight, the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta*—the formal ritual of "making leftover food"—is not required.)

The eight items that a bhikṣu must carry with him (from the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*): 1. the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), 2. the seven-strip robe (*saptaka-uttarāsaṅga*), 3. the five-strip robe (*pañcaka-antarvāsaka*), 4.
the alms bowl (*pātra*), 5. the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), 6. the water strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*), 7. needle and thread, and 8. a small axe (*kuṭhāraka*).

The eight consciousnesses are: first, the eye-consciousness; second, the ear-consciousness; third, the nose-consciousness; fourth, the tongue-consciousness; fifth, the body-consciousness; sixth, the mental-consciousness;
seventh, the transmitting-consciousness; and eighth, the ālaya-consciousness.

The Eight Characteristics of Having Sufficient Food (*Saṃghāṭī*, *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*): 1. Sufficient by self-will; 2. Sufficient by few desires; 3. Sufficient by defilement; 4. Sufficient by mixture; 5.
Sufficient by lack of convenience; 6. Sufficient by flattery and crookedness; 7. Sufficient by staying; 8. Sufficient by one's own self.

The eight perversions (*aṣṭa-mithyātva*) are: first, perversion of view; second, perversion of thought; third, perversion of speech; fourth, perversion of action; fifth, perversion of livelihood; sixth, perversion of diligence;
seventh, perversion of mindfulness; and eighth, perversion of concentration.

Regarding the eight types of stupas (*aṣṭavidha-caitya*): according to the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, the stupa of a Buddha has eight tiers, that of a Bodhisattva has seven tiers, and that of one who has attained the three stages [of the Śrāvaka] has six tiers.
Four [kinds of kings] have four fruits; five [kinds] have five fruits; three [kinds] have three fruits; four [kinds] have two fruits; six [kinds] have one fruit;
seven [kinds] have the first fruit; eight [kinds] have two fruits;

and the Wheel-Turning King has one fruit. Regarding the eight types of coins (in four categories): first, gold; second, silver; third, copper; fourth, iron; fifth, white tin; sixth, lead and pewter; seventh... [text ends].
Wood (8): lacquer.
The eight kinds of musical instruments (according to the *Qingzhong yi*): 1. Metal (bells and chimes); 2. Stone (stone chimes); 3. Silk (zithers and lutes); 4. Bamboo (panpipes and flutes);
5. Gourd (the *konghou*); 6. Earth (the *xuan*); 7. Leather (various drums); 8. Wood (the *zhuzhu* and *yuyu*).
The eight kinds of syrups are: first, pear; second, sour jujube; third, sugarcane; fourth, *vīra* fruit;
fifth, grape; sixth, *śāluka*; seventh, *jambu* fruit; and eighth, *pālaka* fruit.
The eight kinds of bhikṣus (note on the precepts): first, those by name; second, those by resemblance; third, those by self-claim; fourth, those by begging;
fifth, those who wear cut-and-sewn robes; sixth, those who have destroyed the fetters; seventh, those who were "Welcome" (Svāgata); and eighth, those who received full ordination.
The eight kinds of signs (*sujāta*): (1) mountain, (2) rock, (3) grove, (4) tree, (5) path, (6) river, (7) ant mound, (8) water.
The eight kinds of causes and conditions for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe (*caturbhāga*): (1) departure, (2) completion, (3) non-completion, (4) loss, (5) severance of hope.
Sixth, hearing; seventh, exiting the boundary; eighth, exiting together.
There are eight kinds of superior couches (*āgama*): first, a gold couch; second, a silver couch; third, an ivory couch; fourth, a horned couch;
fifth, a Buddha’s couch; sixth, a Teacher’s couch; seventh, a father’s couch; eighth, a mother’s couch.
The Eight Kinds of Faults Regarding Robes (*Vinayavibhāṣā-śāstra*): 1. Completion; 2. Accomplishment; 3. Departure; 4. Loss; 5. Hearing; 6.
Transgressing the Stage; 7. Severance of Expectation; 8. Common Eradication.

The eight methods for assembling the Saṃgha are: first, measuring the shadow; second, splitting bamboo to make a sound; third, striking the ground to make a sound; fourth, producing smoke; fifth, blowing the conch shell;
sixth, beating a drum; seventh, striking the ghaṇṭā; and eighth, announcing that the time for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa has arrived.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* enumerates eight kinds of non-informative action (*avijñapti*): first, simultaneous non-informative action; second, non-informative action of both genders;

third, non-informative action while the object remains present; fourth, non-informative action arising from usage; fifth, non-informative action through a different object-condition; sixth, non-informative action through auxiliary conditions;
seventh, non-informative action through formal commitment; and eighth, non-informative action that follows the mind.
Regarding the eight types of *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) in this Vinaya: first, we may perform the extensive recitation;
second, we may not perform the extensive recitation, but may proceed to the ninety-three [rules]; third, we may not recite the ninety [rules], but may proceed to the thirty-four [rules];

fourth, we may not recite the thirty [rules], but may proceed to the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules; fifth, we may not recite the two *aniyata* rules, but may proceed to the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa] rules; sixth...
One must not explain thirteen items when only four matters or seven items are permitted; one must not explain four matters when only the preface of the *Prātimokṣa* is permitted;
and one must not explain the preface when rising from one's seat to depart.
Eight Circumstances in Which One Need Not Rely [upon a Teacher] (*Shisao*): 1. Seeking tranquility; 2. Guarding one’s dwelling place; 3. Being ill; 4. Attending to the sick; 5.
Having completed five years of practice and achieving virtuous conduct; 6. Possessing wisdom and conduct oneself such that no one superior to oneself resides in the dwelling;
7. An era of famine where food is unavailable; 8. Practicing the Way according to one’s own inclinations.
The eight types of mind for relinquishing the elements (*dhātu*) (from the *Jieshu*): first, the mind of longing and aversion; second, the mind of equanimity; third, the mind of determination;
fourth, the mind abiding in its own nature; fifth, the mind of long-term reflection; sixth, the mind of joy; seventh, the mind of self-possession; eighth, the mind of tranquility.
The Eightfold Noble Path: 1. Right View; 2. Right Intention (wisdom); 3. Right Speech; 4. Right Action; 5.
Right Livelihood (morality); 6. Right Effort; 7. Right Mindfulness; 8. Right Concentration (meditative absorption).
The Tathāgata’s fulfillment of the Way through the eight phases: first, dwelling in Tuṣita; second, descending into the mother’s womb; third, birth; fourth, departing the city;
fifth, subduing Māra; sixth, attaining enlightenment; seventh, preaching the Dharma; eighth, entering parinirvāṇa.
The eight treasuries are: first, the Womb-Birth Treasury; second, the Intermediate State Treasury; third, the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Treasury; fourth, the Vinaya Treasury;
fifth, the Fifty Stages of the Bodhisattva Treasury; sixth, the Miscellaneous Treasury; seventh, the Vajra Treasury; and eighth, the Buddha Treasury.
The eight great hells (according to the Āgamas): first, Saṃjīva; second, Kālasūtra; third, Saṃghāta; fourth, Raurava;
fifth, Mahāraurava; sixth, Tapana; seventh, Pratāpana; eighth, Avīci.
The eight delicacies are: first, rice; second, wheat flour; third, salt; fourth, vinegar; fifth, plums; sixth, crabapples; seventh, mustard seeds; and eighth, ginger. The eight difficulties are:
first, the hells; second, the hungry ghosts; third, the animals; fourth, the long-lived devas; fifth, the northern continent (Uttarakuru); sixth, being born before or after a Buddha;
seventh, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence; and eighth, having impaired faculties.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) permits the abbreviated recitation of the precepts (*saṃkṣipta-poṣadha*) due to eight other circumstances: first, kings; second, bandits; third, water; fourth, fire; fifth, illness;
sixth, non-human beings (*amanuṣya*); seventh, harmful insects; eighth, human difficulties—meaning there is a person who intends to seize and bind a bhikṣu.
The eight hot hells (*Dazhidu lun*): 1. Pit of Charcoal; 2. Boiling Urine; 3. Burning Forest; 4. Forest of Swords; 5. Path of Knives; 6.
Forest of Iron Thorns; 7. Salt River; 8. Copper Stakes.
The eight *pārājika* offenses for bhikṣuṇīs are: first, sexual misconduct; second, theft; third, taking life;

fourth, false speech; fifth, physical contact; sixth, the eight matters (1. grasping the hand; 2. grasping the robe; 3. entering a secluded place; 4. speaking together; 5. standing together; 6. walking together; 7. leaning the body against one another; 8. making an appointment); seventh, concealing [a grave offense];
eighth, following the formal accusation [of another].

The Diagram of the Eight Classes consists of: first, those who have attained the first fruit; second, those who are heading toward the first fruit; third, those who have attained the second fruit; fourth, those who are heading toward the second fruit;

fifth, those who have attained the third fruit; sixth, those who are heading toward the third fruit; seventh, those who have attained the fourth fruit; and eighth, those who are heading toward the fourth fruit.
The Eight Kinds of Impure Wealth (*Shishi Yaolan*): 1. Fields, houses, gardens, and groves; 2. Cultivated plants and seeds for planting;
3. Accumulated grain and silk; 4. Hired servants and laborers; 5. Tethered birds and beasts; 6. Money, jewels, and precious objects; 7.
Carpets, mats, cauldrons, and cooking pots; 8. Elephants, goldsmiths’ tools, and couches.
The Eight Divisions of Celestial Beings are: first, the devas; second, the nāgas; third, the yakṣas; fourth, the gandharvas;
fifth, the asuras; sixth, the garuḍas; seventh, the kiṃnaras; and eighth, the mahoragas.
The *Siddhārthasāra-sūtra* lists the eight winds as follows: first, gain (favorable); second, loss (adverse); third, defamation (adverse); fourth, praise (favorable); fifth, renown (favorable);
sixth, disparagement (adverse); seventh, suffering (adverse); and eighth, pleasure (favorable).
The eight fields of merit are: first, the field of the Buddha; second, the field of noble beings; third, the field of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*); fourth, the field of the instructor (*ācārya*);
fifth, the field of the Sangha; sixth, the field of the father; seventh, the field of the mother; and eighth, the field of the sick.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra consists of eight sections: first, the pārājika; second, the saṃghāvaśeṣa; third, the two aniyata; fourth, the naiḥsargika-pāyattika;
fifth, the pāyattika; sixth, the pratideśanīya; seventh, the duṣkṛta; and eighth, the seven methods for settling disputes.

A bhikṣu who possesses eight qualities [is qualified to take the person to be disciplined to a layperson's home for confession before the Saṃgha]: (1) being widely learned; (2) being able to skillfully expound the Dharma;
(3) understanding it himself after having expounded it; (4) being able to understand the intentions of others; (5) receiving the words of others; (6) being able to remember and retain them;
(7) being free from omissions or errors; and (8) understanding the deliberations on what is wholesome and unwholesome speech.
The reception of the first eight dharmas: (1) requesting the preceptor; (2) establishing the candidate in the designated place; (3) appointing the ritual master for deportment;

(4) the candidate leaving the assembly to answer difficult questions; (5) the formal motion (*jñapti*) to summon the candidate back in; (6) the candidate formally requesting the precepts before the assembly; (7) the ritual master making the formal motion for consensus; (8) the candidate answering difficult questions before the assembly.
The eight types of items for exchange (*Saṃghāṭī*, *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*): first, items [received] at once; second, items [received] during the night period; third, items [received] for seven days;
fourth, items [received] for life; fifth, personal belongings; sixth, heavy items; seventh, impure items; eighth, items that are both pure and impure.
There are nine circumstances for eating apart from the community: first, during illness; second, during the distribution of robes; third, while making robes; fourth, while traveling on a road;
fifth, while traveling by boat; sixth, during a great assembly; seventh, when a gift is offered to śramaṇas; eighth, regarding robes (according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*);
ninth, according to the turn of the saṃgha (according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*).

In the Buddha’s time at Śrāvastī, there were nine hundred million people (according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*): three hundred million households saw the Buddha with their eyes, three hundred million households heard of him but did not see him, and three hundred million households neither heard of nor saw him.
The Nine Meanings of Vinaya (from the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-śāstra*): 1. Bhikṣu-vinaya, such as the emission of semen and so forth; 2.
Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, such as the precept against walking alone and so forth; 3. Ubhaya-vinaya (the Vinaya of both orders), such as the four offenses beginning with sexual misconduct as studied;

4. Āpatti-vinaya (the Vinaya of offenses), such as the eight origins of offenses and so forth; 5. Kleśa-vinaya (the Vinaya of afflictions), such as the afflictions of the three realms and their three grades.

Sixth, those with vows, such as the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera; seventh, those without vows, such as the various precepts following the completion of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, which arise simultaneously;

eighth, the Vinaya regarding time and place, such as receiving the five [precepts] in border regions; ninth, those pertaining to all places, such as killing and stealing, which should be studied together at all times and in all places.
The Seven and Nine Methods of Discipline (Saṃgha-netra): 1. Reprimand; 2. Banishment; 3. Dependence; 4. Prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople;
5. Refusal to acknowledge an offense; 6. Refusal to repent for an offense; 7. Declaring that one’s desires do not obstruct the Path;
8. Treatment of the "evil horse"; 9. Silent banishment.
The nine fetters are: first, craving; second, anger; third, pride; fourth, ignorance; fifth, vexation; sixth, envy; seventh, delusion; eighth, views;
and ninth, grasping.
The nine successive attainments are: first, the concentration of the first dhyāna; second, the concentration of the second dhyāna; third, the concentration of the third dhyāna;

fourth, the concentration of the fourth dhyāna; fifth, the concentration of the sphere of infinite space; sixth, the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness; seventh, the concentration of the sphere of nothingness;
eighth, the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and ninth, the concentration of the cessation of feeling and perception.
There are nine matters for which one should not sit in a layperson’s home: (1) although one performs prostrations, the mind lacks reverence;

(2) although one goes out to welcome them, the mind lacks earnest respect; (3) although one yields a seat to them, the mind is not sincere; (4) one causes them to sit in a place that is disrespectful;
(5) when there is spoken Dharma, the mind does not attend to it; (6) although one hears of their virtues, [one does not rejoice].
Seventh, although one has much to offer, if upon being asked for a small amount, one provides coarse food instead of fine food;
eighth, even when providing what is required, it is done according to the manner of a marketplace transaction.
The three [types of action] multiplied by three make nine kinds (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): first, body; second, speech; third, mind; fourth, performing it oneself; fifth, instructing others;
sixth, rejoicing in seeing them performed; seventh, retribution in the present life; eighth, retribution in the next life; ninth, retribution in subsequent lives.

The nine types of loss of reliance (*niśraya*) according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya): 1. death; 2. departing to a distant place; 3. abandoning the path; 4. committing a grave offense; 5. the teacher being subject to censure; 6.
[the student] being within the boundary of the eight precepts; 7. having completed five years of summer retreat; 8. seeing one’s original *upādhyāya*; 9.
returning [to dwell under the supervision of the *upādhyāya*].
The nine kinds of unrighteousness are: first, quarreling with oneself; second, inciting strife among others; third, inconsistent and contradictory disputes;
fourth, associating with evil friends; fifth, keeping company with wicked people; sixth, delighting in committing evil oneself;
seventh, violating the precepts; eighth, violating right view; and ninth, associating with laypeople.
The Nine Abodes of Sentient Beings (*Abhidharma-śāstra*): the humans and devas of the desire realm in their happy destinies; the first three stages of the form realm;
the non-percipient beings and the first three stages of the formless realm; and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra consists of nine sections and three inquiries: first, the Introduction; second, the Pārājika rules;
third, the Saṃghāvaśeṣa rules; fourth, the two Aniyata rules; fifth, the Naiḥsargika-Pāyattika rules; sixth, the Pāyattika rules; seventh, the Pratideśanīya rules; eighth, the Śaikṣa rules;
and ninth, the Seven Methods for Settling Disputes.

The nine contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*): 1. The contemplation of bloating (*vyādhmātaka-saṃjñā*): [the corpse] is swollen like a leather bag filled with wind. 2. The contemplation of lividness (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*): the skin and flesh are yellowish-red, mottled black, and bluish-green. 3. The contemplation of disintegration (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*):

blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, it is torn and broken apart upon the ground. 4. The contemplation of blood-staining (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*): pus and blood overflow, defiling and coating everything. 5. The contemplation of festering (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*):

worms and pus flow out, and the skin and flesh rot away. 6. The contemplation of being devoured (*vikhāditaka-saṃjñā*): maggots and worms feast upon it; birds peck out its eyes, while foxes, dogs, tigers, and wolves chew, gnaw, and tear it apart. 7. The contemplation of scattering (*vikṣiptaka-saṃjñā*): tendons are severed and bones are separated.

8. The visualization of the bones scattered in disarray (the head and hands are crossed; the white bones and sinews are connected yet dispersed in a state of chaotic disorder); 9. The visualization of burning (the body bursts apart, smoke subsides, the fuel is exhausted, and the form is extinguished, becoming identical to ashes and dust).
The nine sores (also known as the nine apertures, nine entrances, nine leakages, or nine flows): (1–2) the two eyes; (3–4) the two ears; (5–6) the two nostrils;
(7) the mouth; (8) the great path; (9) the small path.
The nine generations: first, Han; second, Wei; third, Jin; fourth, Song; fifth, Qi; sixth, Liang; seventh, Chen; eighth, Sui; ninth, Tang.
The nine paths: first, animals; second, hungry ghosts; third, hell-beings; fourth, asuras; fifth, humans; sixth, devas;
seventh, śrāvakas; eighth, pratyekabuddhas; ninth, bodhisattvas.

The Nine Rules for Kneeling and Sitting (Three Thousand Dignified Manners): 1. Shifting one foot forward or back; 2. Spreading the feet wide apart; 3. Swaying the body; 4. Standing on tiptoe; 5. Crossing the legs; 6.
Leaving the three robes hanging so they do not cover the feet; 7. [Blank]; 8. Stacking the feet; 9. Stacking the thighs.
The Nine Causes of Premature Death for the Sick (*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*): 1. Knowing that food is not beneficial, yet greedily consuming it; 2. Not knowing how to exercise moderation; 3.

Consuming food before what was previously eaten has been digested; 4. Vomiting out food before it has been digested; 5. Forcefully retaining food that has already been digested and should be excreted;
6. Consuming food that does not accord with one’s illness; 7. Consuming food that accords with one’s illness without exercising moderation; 8. Laziness.
Laxity lacks the nine grades of wisdom.
Regarding the nine grades of bowing (*bai*; according to the *Zhouli*: 1. *Jishou*—bowing with the head touching the ground; 2. *Dunshou*—the head striking the ground; 3.

*Kongshou*—the head reaching the hands, meaning the bowing of the head; 4. *Zhendong*—bowing while trembling; 5. *Jibai*—bowing followed by touching the forehead [in mourning], performed for auspicious matters; 6. *Xiongbai*—bowing after touching the forehead [in mourning], performed for three years of mourning).

7. *fú* (the bow of those in mourning); 8. *qí bài* (the single prostration, in response to the bow of subordinates); 9. *bǎo bài* (the double prostration); 10. *sù bài* (the bow performed by lowering the hands).

The nine grades of the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*): the three upper grades (the uppermost-upper grade has twenty-five strips; the upper-middle grade has twenty-three strips; the upper-lower grade has twenty-one strips);

the three middle grades (the middle-upper grade has nineteen strips; the middle-middle grade has seventeen strips; the middle-lower grade has fifteen strips); and the three lower grades (the lower-upper grade has thirteen strips;
the lower-middle grade has eleven strips; the lower-lower grade has nine strips).
The nine grades of receiving the precepts: the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the full precepts (each having three grades—superior, middling, and inferior).

The nine grades of *karmavācanā* procedures (*Karmasūtra*): the three methods of mental recitation (*cittamanasikāra-dharma*) [the method of mental recitation for the assembly, the method of mental recitation for a confessor, and the method of solitary mental recitation];

the three methods of face-to-face confession (*pratyakṣa-dharma*) [the method of face-to-face confession for a small group, the method of face-to-face confession for the assembly, and the method of simple face-to-face confession]; and the three methods concerning sentient beings [the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-mātra-karman*].
The stream of those who possess supernormal powers consists of nine grades (*karma-sūtra*): three grades of superior faculties (superior-superior, superior-middle, superior-inferior);
three grades of middling faculties (middling-superior, middling-middle, middling-inferior); and three grades of inferior faculties (inferior-superior, inferior-middle, inferior-inferior).
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, observing the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) yields nine benefits:
(1) the ten-night period for extra robes; (2) the six-night period; (3) the one-night period; (4) being separated from one's robes;
(5) eating at will; (6) eating repeatedly; and (7) forming a separate assembly.

To inspire faith in those who have not yet believed; 5. To increase the faith of those who already believe;

Ten benefits of wearing rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) that cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): 1. To inspire a sense of shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*). 2. To provide protection against cold, heat, and venomous insects. 3.

To manifest the outward appearance and ritual conduct of a *śramaṇa*. 4. To cause all devas and humans to regard the dharma-robe with singular reverence, as if it were a stūpa. 5. To foster a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*) toward worldly attachments.
1. One dyes the robes not out of a desire for beauty; 2. One conforms to tranquility rather than the blazing of afflictions;
3. By wearing the Dharma-robes, one's evil becomes easily seen; 4. There is no further need for other objects of adornment; 5. One follows the Eightfold Noble Path; 6.
I shall practice the path with diligent application, and will not, for even a moment, allow my mind to be defiled by passion.
The Ten Benefits of Wearing a Garment of Filth (*Daśavihāra-vibhāṣā*): 1. One does not associate with householders for the sake of clothing. 2.
One does not manifest the appearance of begging for clothing for the sake of clothing. 3. Nor does one artfully suggest the acquisition of clothing. 4.

One does not engage in improper seeking in the four directions for the sake of clothing. 5. If one does not obtain clothing, one does not grieve. 6. If one obtains [clothing], [one remains equanimous].

Furthermore, one does not take pleasure in the seven base things because they are easily obtained and free from faults; eighth, one practices in accordance with the four reliances received at the outset;
ninth, one enters among those who wear coarse clothing (meaning one enters the ascetic practice [dhūta] of wearing rag-robes); tenth, one is not greedily attached to by others.
There are ten benefits to receiving garments made of coarse wool (*śāṇa-cīvara*): (1) they are counted among the category of coarse clothing; (2) there is little need for seeking or begging;
(3) one may sit upon them as one pleases; (4) one may lie down upon them as one pleases; (5) they are easy to wash; (6) they are also easy to dye;
(7) they are rarely damaged by insects; (8) they are difficult to destroy; (9) one does not receive other garments again; (10) one does not lose the pursuit of the Way.
The ten benefits for one who possesses only the three robes (*traicīvarika*) (from the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): first, no exhaustion from seeking or receiving anything beyond the three robes;
second, no exhaustion from guarding possessions; third, having few belongings; fourth, being content with what is worn on the body alone; fifth, refining one’s conduct according to the precepts;
sixth, moving about without encumbrance; seventh, physical lightness and agility; eighth, dwelling in accordance with forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*).
9. Dwelling in various places without attachment or concern; 10. Practicing in accordance with the Path.
Regarding the ten benefits of begging for food (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): 1. One’s livelihood is maintained by one's own means and does not depend on others;

2. Those who give me food are caused to abide in the Three Jewels before I eat; 3. Those who give me food shall give rise to a heart of compassion. 4. [The fourth point follows: ... (text fragmentary)
1. To practice in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings; 2. To be easy to satisfy and easy to support; 3. To practice the six dharmas that destroy arrogance; 4.
To possess the roots of goodness of the "unseen crown"; 5. To cause those who see me begging for alms to emulate me in cultivating wholesome dharmas;
6. To have no worldly affairs or entanglements with men, whether young or old; 7. To beg for alms in successive order, giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
The Ten Benefits of *Saṃghāṭī* Congee (*Śīla-śū*): First, complexion; second, strength; third, longevity; fourth, happiness; fifth, clarity of speech and eloquence;
sixth, elimination of food stored overnight; seventh, alleviation of wind-disorders; eighth, digestion of hunger; ninth, quenching of thirst; tenth, regulation of the large and small intestines.
The ten benefits of not consuming food at improper times (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): first, not eating excessively; second, not eating to fullness;
third, not craving delicious flavors; fourth, having few desires and cravings; fifth, having few obstacles and afflictions; sixth, having little illness; seventh, being easily satisfied;
eighth, being easy to support; ninth, possessing contentment; tenth, the body not becoming exhausted from meditation and recitation.
The Ten Benefits of Eating in a Single Sitting (*Daśavihāra-vibhāṣā*): 1. There is no fatigue or distress from seeking a second meal.

2. That which is received is light and small in quantity. 3. There is no fatigue or distress regarding its consumption. 4. There is no fatigue or distress before the meal. 5. One enters the practice of the refined method of eating.
6. One eats after the previous meal has been digested. 7. There are few obstructions or afflictions. 8. There is little illness. 9. The body [is maintained].
The ten kinds of ease and happiness of lightness and convenience;
the ten benefits of sitting according to [seniority] (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): first, no exhaustion from seeking to dwell in a fine vihāra;
second, no exhaustion from seeking fine bedding; third, not troubling the seniors; fourth, not causing juniors to feel sorrow or distress; fifth, having few desires.

Sixth, having few affairs; seventh, obtaining what is needed and using it; eighth, using little and thus having few responsibilities; ninth, not giving rise to causes for dispute; tenth, not seizing what others use.

(The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* on the ten benefits of sitting in a charnel ground: First, one constantly attains the perception of impermanence; second, one attains the perception of death; third, one attains...
1. The perception of impurity; 2. The perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in; 3. Constantly being able to remain far removed from all beloved persons;
4. Constantly possessing a heart of compassion; 5. Remaining far removed from frivolity and playfulness; 6. A mind that is constantly weary of and detached from [saṃsāra];
7. Diligently practicing vigor; 8. Being able to eliminate fear.
The Ten Benefits of Sitting Beneath a Tree (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): 1. There is no weariness from seeking a dwelling; 2. There is no weariness from seeking bedding and furniture;
3. There is no weariness from what is cherished; 4. There is no weariness from material enjoyments;

5. There is no place for a name [to be established]; 6. There are no matters of contention; 7. One accords with the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*); 8. It is easily obtained and free from [worldly] attachments.
Beyond the nine stages that accord with the path of cultivation, there is the tenth stage: the practice of dwelling in a place free from the clamor of crowds.

This is the "Always Sitting and Not Reclining" (常坐不臥), which possesses ten benefits (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): first, not craving the pleasure of the body; second, not craving the pleasure of sleep; third, not craving the pleasure of bedding;
fourth, being free from the suffering of the side pressing against the mat during the time of reclining; fifth, not following the desires of the body.
Sixth, it is easy to obtain a place for sitting in meditation; seventh, it is easy to read and recite the sutras; eighth, one sleeps little; ninth, the body is light and rises easily;
tenth, the mind is detached from seeking seats, bedding, or clothing.
(From the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*): First, not seeking shelter under trees; second, being far removed from what belongs to the self; third, having no... [text fragment].

1. There are no legal disputes; 2. one departs from others without looking back with regret; 3. there is little frivolous joking; 4. one is able to endure wind, rain, venomous insects, cold, and heat;
5. one is not pierced by sounds or thorns; 6. one does not cause sentient beings to harbor anger or resentment;
7. one is oneself free from sorrow and hatred; 8. there is no place where one dwells amidst the clamor of crowds.
The ten benefits for a bhikṣu practicing in the forest (*araṇya*) (from the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*): first, coming and going with mastery; second, being free from the notions of "self" and "mine";
third, moving according to one's will without obstruction; fourth, the mind delighting in the practice of dwelling in empty places; fifth, having few desires and few affairs regarding one’s dwelling;
sixth, not sparing body or life for the sake of perfecting merit; seventh, remaining far removed from clamorous speech; eighth, although practicing meritorious deeds, not seeking gratitude or reward.

Ninth, being compliant with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one easily attains a single-pointed mind. Tenth, dwelling in the sphere of empty space (*ākāśāyatana*), one easily gives rise to the perception of non-obstruction.

Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*): first, the power of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*); second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration; fourth, the power of the faculties (*indriya*);

fifth, the power of aspiration (*chanda*); sixth, the power of disposition (*gotra*); seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); ninth, the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); tenth, the power regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Exerting one's full effort. The eleven factors (*abhidharma*): 1. Mindfulness of the body; 2. Concentration and wisdom; 3. Concentration with directed thought and evaluation, and concentration without directed thought and evaluation;

4. The three liberations; 5. The four foundations of mindfulness; 6. The four right efforts; 7. The four bases of psychic power; 8. The five faculties; 9. The five powers; 10. [The seven factors of enlightenment]; 11. The Noble Eightfold Path.

Six: The Six Recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti). Seven: The Seven Factors of Enlightenment (sapta-bodhyaṅga). Eight: The Eightfold Noble Path (āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga). Nine: The Nine Successive Attainments (navānupūrva-samāpatti).

Ten: The Ten Totalities (daśa-kṛtsnāyatana; also known as the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*). Eleven: The Eleven Knowledges (ekādaśa-jñāna; also known as the eleven *sarvajñatās*): 1. Knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*). 2. Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). 3. Knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

4. Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). 5. Knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). 6. Knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*). 7. Knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). 8. Knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). 9. [Knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)]. 10. [Knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)]. 11. [Knowledge of others' faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñāna*)].
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is the tenth, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is the eleventh, and the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtajñāna*) is the twelfth.

Regarding the different ways of receiving robes during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, there are eleven types of persons (as recorded in the *Zizhi*): first, one who has granted consent (*chanda*); second, one who is facing difficulties;

third, one who lacks the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*); fourth, one from a different boundary (*sīmā*); fifth, one who observes the middle or later retreat; sixth, one who has broken [the precepts]; seventh, one who has not performed the formal ritual (*anupasaṃpanna*); eighth, one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Nine: *parivāsa* (probation); ten: *śikṣādattaka* (one undergoing penance);

eleven: *pravāsanīya* (one to be expelled). Twelve: the links of dependent origination—1. ignorance (*avidyā*), 2. volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) (past causes); 3. consciousness (*vijñāna*), 4. name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), 5.

the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), 6. contact (*sparśa*), 7. feeling (*vedanā*) (present effects); 8. craving (*tṛṣṇā*), 9. grasping (*upādāna*), 10. existence (*bhava*) (present causes); 11. birth (*jāti*), 12. old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) (future effects).

The Method for Striking the *Ghaṇṭī* at the Twelve Hours (*Sāhasraka-vaipulya-vinaya*, Five Thousand Forms of Dignified Conduct): Five Commonly Used Methods. 1. At the time of the regular assembly, a total of fifty-four strikes.
2. At the time of the morning meal, eight strikes. 3. At the time of the midday meal, one continuous strike, which is fifty-four strikes.
4. At the time of evening offerings, likewise one continuous strike. 5. At the time of impermanence (*anityatā*), the number of strikes varies according to the occasion. The Sevenfold [Method].

The sequence of the rites is as follows: first, the Dharma; second, the county magistrate; third, great fire; fourth, great water; fifth, bandits (the frequency of these from one to four varies according to the occasion);

sixth, the assembly of śrāmaṇeras, three times with the *xià* (lower) tone; seventh, the assembly of upāsakas, twice with the *xià* tone; eighth, calling for private children, once with the *xià* tone.
The Twelve Dhūta Practices (*Shìchāo*): 1. Wearing patched robes; 2. Possessing only the three robes; 3. Constantly begging for food; 4. Not performing the ritual of leaving over food;
5. Eating in a single sitting; 6. Eating in a single mouthful; 7. Dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage); 8. Dwelling among graves; 9. Dwelling at the foot of a tree;
10. Dwelling in the open air; 11. Sitting wherever one happens to be; 12. Constantly sitting without lying down (regarding deportment).
In the *Mahāsāṃghika*, there are twelve persons when four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) are performed interchangeably by separate groups (one walking, two standing, three sitting, four reclining).
If one performs a *karmavācanā* while [the others] are walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, it constitutes a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).

The Twelve Bases (*dvādaśāyatana*; the meaning is that they involve mutual entry between the faculties and their objects; these twelve are named after what is entered). 1. The eye, which is able to see the sphere of form. 2.

The ear, which is able to hear the sphere of sound. 3. The nose, which is able to smell the sphere of fragrance. 4. The tongue, which is able to know the sphere of taste. 5. The body, which is able to perceive the sphere of tangibles. 6.

The mind, which is able to cognize the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharma*). (These are the six internal bases of the faculties. 7. Form, which is the object seen by the eye. 8. Sound... [and so forth].
1. Sounds corresponding to what is heard by the ear; 2. fragrances corresponding to what is smelled by the nose; 3. tastes corresponding to what is tasted by the tongue;
4. tangibles corresponding to what is felt by the body; 5. phenomena corresponding to what is known by the mind (the six external sense objects).
The twelve divisions of the scriptures (Sanskrit-Chinese bilingual): 1. Sūtra (Discourse); 2. Geya (Repetitional Verses);
3. Vyākaraṇa (Prophecy); 4. Gāthā (Verses); 5. Udāna (Unprompted Utterances); 6. Nidāna (Causes and Conditions);
7. Avadāna (Parables); 8. Itivṛttaka (Past Occurrences); 9. Jātaka (Birth Stories); 10. Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings).
11. Adbhutadharma (Marvels); 12. Upadeśa (Exegesis). The twelve divisions of the Vinaya; the twelve divisions of the teachings.
The Sarvāstivāda further split into four schools;
the Vātsīputrīya school further split into three: the Dharmottarīya, the Bhadrayānīya, and the Sammitīya.

the three and the six,
constitute the division of the Kāśyapīya school into two sects.

two branches emerged:

the Mahāsāṃghika school was not divided,
nor was the Dharmaguptaka school divided.
The twelve classes of beings (*Lengyan jing*): 1. egg-born; 2. womb-born; 3. moisture-born; 4. transformation-born;
5. those with form; 6. those without form; 7. those with perception; 8. those without perception; 9.

those who are neither with nor without form; 10. those who are neither with nor without form; 11. those who are neither with nor without perception; 12. those who are neither with nor without perception.
The fourfold precept against stealing consists of thirteen categories: (1) within a single area; (2) on the ground; (3) above the ground; (4) by means of a vehicle; (5) from a shoulder-pole;
(6) from the air; (7) from a loft; (8) from a village; (9) from an araṇya; (10) from a field; (11) from a specific location; (12) from a boat;
and (13) by secretly crossing a frontier or barrier.

The thirteen difficult cases are: first, one who has committed an immediate offense (*ānantarya*); second, one who has defiled a nun; third, one who dwells as a thief; fourth, one who has caused schism between internal and external sects; fifth, a eunuch; sixth, one who has killed his father;

seventh, one who has killed his mother; eighth, one who has killed an Arhat; ninth, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha by destroying the Wheel of Dharma; tenth, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha;
eleventh, a non-human being; twelfth, an animal; and thirteenth, one with two sexual organs.
The fourteen types of form are: (1) color, (2) sound, (3) fragrance, (4) taste, (5) touch (the five objects);
(6) eye, (7) ear, (8) nose, (9) tongue, (10) body (the five faculties); and (11) earth, (12) water, (13) fire, (14) wind (the four great elements).

The Fifteen Brief Expositions of the Precepts (with three additions): 1. Having recited the introduction (*nidāna*), the rest is that which the Saṃgha hears regularly. 2. Having recited up to the four *pārājika* offenses. 3.
Having recited up to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. 4. Having recited up to the two *aniyata* offenses. 5. The full exposition (these five apply to those from the thirty down).

6. Having recited the four *pārājika* offenses. 7. Having recited up to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. 8. Having recited up to the two *aniyata* offenses. 9. Having recited up to the three [niḥsargika-pāyattika] offenses.
10. Having extensively explained ten [cases] (these five from the ninth down to the tenth); 11. Having explained thirteen [cases]; 12. Having reached the two *aniyata* [dharmas];
13. Having reached thirty [cases]; 14. Having reached ninety [cases]; 15. Having extensively explained five [cases] (these five from the *pācittiya* down to the end).

The Fifteen Kinds of Silence (*Saṃyukta-khandhaka*) 1. If one performs a formal act (*kamma*) in accordance with the Dharma; 2. If one has obtained companions who agree; 3. If one sees a minor offense; 4.

If one is performing the *parivāsa* (probation); 5. If one is within the boundary of the *sīmā* (one must not remain silent); 6. If one sees another acting contrary to the Dharma; 7. If one does not obtain companions; 8.
If one has committed a grave offense (*pārājika*); 9. If one is living in communal residence (*sahavāsa*); 10. If one is in a place where communal residence is established.
11. [One should remain] silent; 12. [If it is] in accordance with the Dharma, one should remain silent and acquiesce; 13. [One may] give consent (*chanda*);
14. [Or] hear from a trustworthy person; 15. One should first sit silently within the assembly [so that the community] may be in harmony.

The fifteen natural boundaries (*prakṛti-sīmā*) are: first, the boundary of a monastery; second, the boundary of a village; third, the boundary of a grove of trees; fourth, the boundary of a threshing floor; fifth, the boundary of a cart caravan;

sixth, the boundary of a boat; seventh, the boundary of a house; eighth, the boundary of a hall; ninth, the boundary of a storehouse; tenth, the boundary of a granary; eleventh, the boundary of an araṇya (forest hermitage);

The afflictions of the three realms comprise fifteen categories in total (*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*): (1) fetters to be abandoned by insight; (2) fetters to be abandoned by [the path of] accumulation;
(3) fetters to be abandoned by [the path of] cessation; (4) fetters to be abandoned by [the path of] cultivation; and (5) fetters to be abandoned by cultivation.
Each of these pertains to all three realms: desire, form, and formlessness.

There are eighty-one grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*): [those of] the desire realm, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and [the formless realms of] space, consciousness, and nothingness.
All [afflictions] other than those of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (each having nine grades) are divided into nine stages within the three realms;
within each stage there are nine grades of delusion, totaling eighty-one grades.
The eighty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*):

in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), all ten afflictions are present; under the truths of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), the afflictions of self-view (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and views of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) are excluded.

Under the four truths of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the same pattern applies, with the exception of [the exclusion of] self-view and views of extremes; thus, they collectively constitute thirty-two [afflictions]. The formulation for each of the four truths in the form and formless realms is identical to that of the desire realm.
In the [form] realm, with the exception of the latent tendency of hatred (*pratighānuśaya*), it differs from the former realm;
there are twenty-eight [factors] in one realm, and when two realms are combined, there are fifty-six. Adding the thirty-two of the preceding desire realm, they total eighty-eight.
Now, regarding the Master’s method for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), there are two hundred and ten types.

The total number of types is two hundred and ten. According to the methods for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) of the ancient masters, there are one hundred and sixty types (*Karmavastu-śūtra* states:
"Some say that since the first two methods possess scriptural authority, they may be applied across all three seasons; thus, [the others] are forgotten").

Furthermore, regarding these five dharmas of the *dharmapada* (formal procedures), because they are established through formal enactment (*karmavācanā*) and are originally beyond verbal expression, they are not permitted during the mid-year retreat (*antarvarṣa*).
Thus, according to this numerical reckoning, there are one hundred and sixty types:

the first two dharmas, when applied across the three periods, the two locations, and the five assemblies, result in sixty types; the latter five dharmas, based on the preceding two periods, result in one hundred.
